title: Nonuniqueness for x' = sqrt(|x|) at the Origin
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The initial value problem x' = sqrt(|x|), x(0) = 0 has infinitely many solutions: the zero solution and solutions that stay at zero until an arbitrary time c and then depart.
latex: x'=\sqrt{|x|},\ x(0)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(t)=0 \text{ or } x(t)=\tfrac14(t-c)^2\ (t\ge c)
short: Hölder continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness.
long: Hölder continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness. For each c >= 0 the piecewise function is C^1 and solves the equation; Peano's theorem still guarantees existence.
proof: Separate variables on x>0 to get 2 sqrt(x)=t-c, then check C^1 matching at t=c; the right-hand side fails Lipschitz continuity at 0.
consequence: The Lipschitz hypothesis in Picard–Lindelöf cannot simply be weakened to continuity.

title: Integrating Factor for First-Order Linear ODEs
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For y' + p(t)y = q(t) with p continuous, multiplying by mu(t) = exp(integral p) makes the left side an exact derivative and yields the general solution.
short: An exponential multiplier collapses the left side into one derivative.
long: An exponential multiplier collapses the left side into one derivative. The factor satisfies mu'/mu = p, so the product rule reduces the equation to a single integration.
proof: Compute (mu y)' = mu(y'+py) = mu q, integrate, and divide by the positive function mu.
consequence: It gives explicit solutions of all first-order linear ODEs and motivates variation of constants.

title: Bernoulli Equation Substitution
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The Bernoulli equation y' + p(t)y = q(t)y^n with n not 0 or 1 becomes linear under u = y^(1-n).
short: A power substitution linearises a classical nonlinear equation.
long: A power substitution linearises a classical nonlinear equation. Divide by y^n and use u' = (1-n)y^{-n}y' to obtain a linear equation for u.
proof: Differentiate the substitution and substitute; the resulting linear equation is solved by an integrating factor.
consequence: It extends explicit solvability to a useful family of nonlinear first-order equations.

title: Riccati Equation Linearisation
subject: Differential Equations
statement: A scalar Riccati equation y' = a(t) + b(t)y + c(t)y^2 with c nonzero transforms into a second-order linear equation for u via y = -u'/(cu).
short: Riccati equations are the nonlinear shadow of linear second-order equations.
long: Riccati equations are the nonlinear shadow of linear second-order equations. Any nonvanishing solution u of the linear equation recovers a Riccati solution, and one known particular solution reduces the Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation.
proof: Differentiate y = -u'/(cu), substitute into the Riccati equation, and simplify.
consequence: Special-function solutions of linear equations transfer to nonlinear Riccati problems.

title: Euler–Cauchy Equation Power Solutions
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The Cauchy–Euler equation t^2 y'' + alpha t y' + beta y = 0 on t>0 has power solutions y = t^r whose exponents solve a quadratic indicial equation.
latex: t^2y''+\alpha t y'+\beta y=0,\quad r(r-1)+\alpha r+\beta=0,\quad y=t^r
short: Scaling invariance turns a variable-coefficient equation into algebra.
long: Scaling invariance turns a variable-coefficient equation into algebra. A repeated root gives the second solution t^r log t; complex roots give t^a cos(b log t) and t^a sin(b log t).
proof: Insert y=t^r and collect powers of t; the two roots give independent solutions by the Wronskian.
consequence: It is the model equation for scaling symmetry and singular endpoints.

title: Abel's Identity for the Wronskian
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = 0 the Wronskian of two solutions satisfies W(t) = W(t0) exp(-integral of p from t0 to t).
short: The Wronskian obeys a first-order equation of its own.
long: The Wronskian obeys a first-order equation of its own. It depends only on the coefficient of y', not on q.
proof: Differentiate W and use the ODE for both solutions; the q-terms cancel, leaving W' = -pW.
consequence: The Wronskian either vanishes everywhere or nowhere, settling independence immediately.

title: Floquet Theory for Periodic Coefficients
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For x' = A(t)x with A(t+T) = A(t), every fundamental matrix has the form P(t)exp(Rt) with P periodic; stability is governed by the eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix.
short: Periodic coefficients impose a multiplier structure like constant coefficients.
long: Periodic coefficients impose a multiplier structure like constant coefficients. The multipliers are eigenvalues of X(T)X(0)^{-1}; solutions decay when all multipliers lie inside the unit circle.
proof: Since X(t+T) is again a fundamental matrix, X(t+T)=X(t)C; take a matrix logarithm of the nonsingular C.
consequence: It reduces stability of periodically driven systems to one matrix, as in Mathieu and Hill equations.

title: Sturm Comparison Theorem
subject: Differential Equations
statement: If q1 < q2, then between two consecutive zeros of a nontrivial solution of (p y')' + q1 y = 0 there is a zero of every solution of (p z')' + q2 z = 0.
latex: (py')'+q_1y=0,\ (pz')'+q_2z=0,\ q_1<q_2 \Rightarrow z \text{ has a zero between consecutive zeros of } y
short: A more oscillatory equation cannot avoid the zeros of a less oscillatory one.
long: A more oscillatory equation cannot avoid the zeros of a less oscillatory one. The result is a comparison of oscillation, not of solution values or amplitudes.
proof: Integrate p(y'z - yz')' = (q1-q2)yz between consecutive zeros of y; a constant-sign assumption on z gives a contradiction.
consequence: It yields oscillation criteria and eigenvalue separation without solving equations.

title: Green's Function for Two-Point Boundary Value Problems
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For a Dirichlet problem on [a,b] with trivial homogeneous solution, the solution is an integral of a Green function that is continuous, solves the homogeneous equation off the diagonal, and has a prescribed derivative jump.
short: A derivative jump encodes a point source and reconstructs every solution.
long: A derivative jump encodes a point source and reconstructs every solution. For L = -(p y')' + q y the jump follows by integrating L y = delta across s = x.
proof: Assemble G from two homogeneous solutions satisfying the left and right boundary conditions, choose the jump, then integrate by parts to verify.
consequence: It converts boundary value problems into integral equations and exposes spectral structure.

title: Bendixson–Dulac Criterion for Planar Systems
subject: Differential Equations
statement: If a C^1 function B on a simply connected region D makes the divergence of B f of one sign and not identically zero, the planar system z' = f(z) has no periodic orbit lying wholly in D.
short: A signed divergence obstructs the return of a planar trajectory.
long: A signed divergence obstructs the return of a planar trajectory. The choice B = 1 is often enough; other choices handle ecological and circuit models.
proof: By Green's theorem the flux of Bf across a closed orbit equals the integral of its divergence over the enclosed region, which cannot vanish.
consequence: It rules out limit cycles and is a standard planar qualitative tool.

title: Stable Manifold Theorem for Hyperbolic Equilibria
subject: Differential Equations
statement: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium of a C^1 flow, the stable and unstable sets are manifolds tangent to the corresponding eigenspaces of the linearisation, with matching dimensions.
short: Linear spectral information survives locally in the nonlinear flow.
long: Linear spectral information survives locally in the nonlinear flow. The local manifolds are as smooth as the vector field; the global manifolds are their time-evolutes.
proof: Solve an integral equation for graph transforms in exponentially invariant cones using the contraction mapping principle.
consequence: It justifies linearisation-based predictions and organises bifurcation analysis.

title: LaSalle Invariance Principle
subject: Differential Equations
statement: If V is a C^1 Lyapunov function with nonpositive derivative on a compact positively invariant set, trajectories approach the largest invariant subset of the set where V' = 0.
short: Even a non-strict Lyapunov function locates the limiting motion.
long: Even a non-strict Lyapunov function locates the limiting motion. It applies when the derivative vanishes along a whole manifold rather than only at an equilibrium.
proof: V decreases to a limit on the invariant set; on the omega-limit set V is constant, so trajectories there satisfy V' = 0.
consequence: It proves asymptotic stability for damped systems and consensus dynamics.

title: Tikhonov Theorem on Singularly Perturbed Systems
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For x' = f(x,z), epsilon z' = g(x,z) with epsilon going to zero, if the fast equation has a uniformly asymptotically stable equilibrium z = h(x), the slow variables converge to the solution of x' = f(x,h(x)) away from an initial layer.
short: Fast variables relax and leave a reduced slow dynamics.
long: Fast variables relax and leave a reduced slow dynamics. Convergence is uniform on compact time intervals bounded away from t=0.
proof: Introduce fast-time boundary-layer coordinates, establish exponential decay there, and match to the reduced solution.
consequence: It underpins quasi-steady-state approximations in chemistry and control.

title: Method of Multiple Scales
subject: Differential Equations
statement: Treating slow and fast time variables as independent removes secular terms from regular perturbation expansions and yields uniformly valid amplitude equations.
short: Let the solution see two clocks at once.
long: Let the solution see two clocks at once. Expanding x = x0 + epsilon x1 + ... and eliminating resonant terms gives slow evolution equations for amplitudes and phases.
proof: The chain rule gives the expanded derivative operator; solvability conditions remove terms that grow linearly in t.
consequence: It gives uniformly valid approximations for weakly nonlinear oscillators and waves.

title: Van der Pol Relaxation Oscillation
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For large mu the van der Pol oscillator has a limit cycle with slow crawling along the branches of a cubic nullcline interrupted by fast jumps.
short: Strong nonlinear damping produces a cycle with two very different time scales.
long: Strong nonlinear damping produces a cycle with two very different time scales. In Lienard form the slow manifold loses stability at its folds, causing the jumps.
proof: Set y = x - x^3/3 - x'/mu; the critical manifold y = x - x^3/3 has attracting outer branches and a repelling middle branch.
consequence: It is a prototype for excitable systems and early models of cardiac and electrical oscillators.

title: Poincaré–Lindstedt Method
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For weakly nonlinear oscillators whose frequency depends on amplitude, expanding the frequency together with the solution avoids secular terms of regular perturbation theory.
short: Let the clock change with the amplitude.
long: Let the clock change with the amplitude. The coefficient 3/8 applies to the Duffing equation with unit coefficients and oscillation amplitude a.
proof: Put tau = omega t, expand x and omega in epsilon, and set the resonant cos(tau) coefficient to zero.
consequence: It gives accurate periodic solutions where naive series fail at long times.

title: SEIR Epidemic Model and Basic Reproduction Number
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: The SEIR model adds an exposed compartment to SIR; the basic reproduction number is beta/gamma, and the disease-free equilibrium loses stability when it exceeds one.
latex: S'=-\beta SI/N,\ E'=\beta SI/N-\sigma E,\ I'=\sigma E-\gamma I,\quad \mathcal R_0=\beta/\gamma
short: An incubation stage delays but does not change the threshold.
long: An incubation stage delays but does not change the threshold. The mean latent period is 1/sigma; R0 counts infections caused by one infectious individual over the infectious lifetime.
proof: Linearise at the disease-free equilibrium; the next-generation eigenvalue is beta/gamma, giving the stability switch.
consequence: It guides vaccination thresholds and explains delayed epidemic peaks.

title: Next-Generation Matrix and R0
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: For a multi-compartment epidemic model, the next-generation matrix records expected infections across compartment types, and R0 is its spectral radius.
latex: K_{ij}=\text{expected infections in } i \text{ from one infectious in } j,\quad \mathcal R_0=\rho(K)
short: R0 becomes a spectral radius when hosts are heterogeneous.
long: R0 becomes a spectral radius when hosts are heterogeneous. The construction splits new infections from other transitions in the linearised infected subsystem.
proof: Linearise the infected equations, factor K as F V^{-1}, and apply the Perron–Frobenius theorem to the nonnegative matrix.
consequence: It produces threshold conditions for age-structured and multi-strain diseases.

title: Final Size Equation for SIR Epidemics
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: Without births or deaths, the final susceptible fraction in the SIR model satisfies an implicit relation determined by the basic reproduction number and the initial susceptible fraction.
short: The epidemic stops when susceptibles fall below the herd-immunity threshold.
long: The epidemic stops when susceptibles fall below the herd-immunity threshold. The relation is independent of the time course and of the initial number of infectious individuals.
proof: Divide dS/dR = -R0 S/N, integrate, and use I(infinity)=0 to replace R(infinity)-R(0) by S(0)-S(infinity).
consequence: It constrains total epidemic size and underlies herd-immunity calculations.

title: SIS Epidemic Threshold on Contact Networks
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: In the mean-field SIS model on a network, an endemic state appears when beta/gamma exceeds the inverse adjacency spectral radius; heterogeneous degree distributions lower the threshold.
short: Hubs keep an epidemic alive at lower transmission rates.
long: Hubs keep an epidemic alive at lower transmission rates. For scale-free networks with diverging spectral radius the mean-field threshold can vanish.
proof: Linearise the node-level mean-field equations at the disease-free state; the dominant eigenvalue of beta A/gamma decides stability.
consequence: It links topology to disease control and motivates targeted immunisation.

title: Competitive Exclusion in Lotka–Volterra Systems
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: In the two-species Lotka–Volterra competition system, stable coexistence occurs exactly when each interspecific competition coefficient is smaller than the corresponding self-limitation; otherwise one species excludes the other.
short: A niche difference is needed for two consumers to coexist.
long: A niche difference is needed for two consumers to coexist. If both coefficients exceed one the outcome is bistable, with the winner set by initial conditions.
proof: Classify the boundary and interior equilibria by the Jacobian; the interior determinant condition gives coexistence exactly when both alpha are below one.
consequence: It formalises Gause's competitive exclusion principle.

title: Michaelis–Menten Rate Law
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: Under the quasi-steady-state assumption for the enzyme–substrate complex, the reaction velocity is a saturating hyperbola in the substrate concentration.
short: Enzyme kinetics saturates hyperbolically in substrate concentration.
long: Enzyme kinetics saturates hyperbolically in substrate concentration. At substrate concentration equal to Km the reaction runs at half maximal velocity.
proof: Set d[ES]/dt = 0, use enzyme conservation [E]+[ES]=[E]0, and solve for v = kcat[ES].
consequence: It is the standard rate law of biochemistry and systems biology.

title: Turing Instability Reaction–Diffusion
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: A reaction–diffusion system can be stable without diffusion but unstable to spatially modulated perturbations when the activator diffuses more slowly than the inhibitor.
short: Diffusion can create spatial pattern from a homogeneous state.
long: Diffusion can create spatial pattern from a homogeneous state. Instability requires a finite band of wave numbers, selecting a characteristic pattern wavelength.
proof: Linearise in Fourier modes exp(ikx+lambda t); the dispersion relation lambda(k) can have positive real part even when lambda(0) does not.
consequence: It explains stripes and spots in morphogenesis and animal coat patterns.

title: Fisher–KPP Travelling Wave Speed
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: The Fisher–KPP equation has travelling fronts connecting the unstable state to the stable one for all speeds at least 2 sqrt(rD), and steep initial data select that minimal speed.
short: Pulled fronts advance at the linear spreading speed.
long: Pulled fronts advance at the linear spreading speed. Fronts faster than the minimum exist, but compactly supported initial data converge to the minimal-speed front.
proof: Insert u(x-ct), linearise at the leading edge u about zero, and require real decay exponents, giving c at least 2 sqrt(rD).
consequence: It predicts invasion speeds in ecology and spatial epidemiology.

title: Hodgkin–Huxley Conductance Model
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: The Hodgkin–Huxley equations balance membrane capacitance against voltage-gated sodium, potassium, and leak currents, with gating variables obeying voltage-dependent kinetics.
short: An action potential emerges from competing voltage-dependent currents.
long: An action potential emerges from competing voltage-dependent currents. The exponents 3 and 4 come from independently acting sodium activation and potassium activation gates.
proof: Fit gating rate functions to voltage-clamp data and substitute the resulting conductances into the current-balance equation.
consequence: It founded quantitative electrophysiology and inspired simpler excitable models.

title: FitzHugh–Nagumo Oscillator
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: The FitzHugh–Nagumo system reduces excitability to a cubic voltage nullcline and a slow recovery variable, producing a limit cycle for suitable parameters.
short: A two-variable caricature captures threshold and refractoriness.
long: A two-variable caricature captures threshold and refractoriness. For suitable applied current the cubic nullcline's middle branch is unstable and relaxation oscillations result.
proof: Locate the fixed point, check the Jacobian for a Hopf bifurcation, and follow the slow manifold to the cycle.
consequence: It makes excitable dynamics accessible to phase-plane analysis.

title: Keller–Segel Chemotaxis Model
subject: Mathematical Biology
statement: The Keller–Segel system couples cell density to a chemoattractant; in two dimensions there is a critical mass separating global existence from blow-up.
short: Attraction plus diffusion has a sharp mass threshold for aggregation.
long: Attraction plus diffusion has a sharp mass threshold for aggregation. The threshold applies to the parabolic–elliptic simplification with instantaneous chemical equilibration.
proof: The free energy decreases; the Moser–Trudinger inequality gives global existence below the critical mass and construction of blowing-up solutions above it.
consequence: It is the canonical aggregation model and a testing ground for singular PDEs.

title: Fourier Transform Convolution Theorem
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Fourier transform of the convolution of two integrable functions is the pointwise product of their Fourier transforms.
short: Convolution in one domain is multiplication in the other.
long: Convolution in one domain is multiplication in the other. The exact constant depends on the Fourier normalisation convention.
proof: Insert the convolution into the Fourier integral, apply Fubini's theorem, and substitute x = y + z.
consequence: It turns linear filtering into pointwise algebra and enables fast convolution algorithms.

title: Plancherel Theorem for the Fourier Transform
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: With the convention having 2 pi in the exponential, the Fourier transform extends to a unitary operator on L^2 and preserves the inner product.
short: The Fourier transform preserves energy.
long: The Fourier transform preserves energy. The identity first holds for Schwartz functions and then extends by density to all of L^2.
proof: Use the convolution identity at zero, approximate the identity by approximate identities, and pass to the limit.
consequence: It justifies energy-preserving spectral methods and Parseval computations.

title: Fourier Transform of Derivatives
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Differentiation in physical space corresponds to multiplication by 2 pi i xi in frequency space, provided the function decays at infinity.
short: Derivatives become algebraic multipliers in frequency space.
long: Derivatives become algebraic multipliers in frequency space. Boundary terms vanish for Schwartz functions or sufficiently decaying absolutely continuous functions.
proof: Integrate by parts n times, discarding the boundary terms.
consequence: It converts linear differential equations into algebraic equations and defines Sobolev norms.

title: Laplace Transform Convolution Theorem
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The Laplace transform of the causal convolution of two functions of exponential order equals the product of their Laplace transforms.
short: Causal convolution becomes multiplication in Laplace space.
long: Causal convolution becomes multiplication in Laplace space. It is the one-sided analogue of the Fourier convolution theorem.
proof: Write the double integral over the triangle 0 <= u <= t and interchange the order of integration.
consequence: It solves linear ODEs with general forcing by multiplication and inversion.

title: Laplace Transform of Derivatives and Initial Conditions
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The Laplace transform of a derivative is s times the transform of the function minus its initial value, so initial conditions enter algebraically.
short: Initial data appear as subtraction terms in Laplace space.
long: Initial data appear as subtraction terms in Laplace space. Higher derivatives produce a polynomial in s whose coefficients are the initial derivatives.
proof: Integrate by parts in the defining integral of the Laplace transform.
consequence: It reduces initial value problems for linear ODEs to rational algebra.

title: Mellin Transform and Its Scaling Property
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Mellin transform of a dilated function is a power of the dilation factor times the original transform, and multiplying by x corresponds to differentiation in the transform variable.
short: Mellin transforms diagonalise scaling and multiplicative convolution.
long: Mellin transforms diagonalise scaling and multiplicative convolution. The strip of analyticity of M[f] reflects the decay of f at zero and infinity.
proof: Substitute x -> ax for the scaling law and integrate by parts for the derivative identity, assuming boundary terms vanish.
consequence: It solves scale-invariant integral equations and analyses zeta functions and algorithms.

title: Hilbert Transform and the Kramers–Kronig Relations
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For a causal linear response function, the real and imaginary parts of its Fourier transform are related by the Hilbert transform through the Kramers–Kronig dispersion relations.
short: Causality ties dissipation to dispersion.
long: Causality ties dissipation to dispersion. The relations require the response to be analytic in the upper half-plane and to decay sufficiently fast.
proof: Apply Cauchy's theorem to the analytic response and use the Sokhotski–Plemelj formula on the real axis.
consequence: It constrains optical constants and scattering amplitudes from measured data.

title: Projection-Slice Theorem
subject: Signal Processing
statement: The one-dimensional Fourier transform of a parallel-beam projection of a function equals a central slice through the two-dimensional Fourier transform of that function.
short: Radon data and Fourier data are the same object in different coordinates.
long: Radon data and Fourier data are the same object in different coordinates. Collecting slices at all angles fills the Fourier plane in polar coordinates.
proof: Write the line integral in Fourier variables and integrate out the direction perpendicular to the beam, producing a delta function.
consequence: It is the basis of computed tomography reconstruction by filtered back-projection.

title: Poisson Summation Formula
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: For a sufficiently decaying function, the sum over integer values equals the sum of the Fourier transform over the dual integer lattice.
latex: \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f(n)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\hat f(k),\qquad \hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx
short: Periodisation and sampling are Fourier duals.
long: Periodisation and sampling are Fourier duals. General lattices lead to a dual lattice determined by the inverse transpose.
proof: Periodise f, expand the resulting function in a Fourier series, and compute the coefficients.
consequence: It links theta functions, lattice sums, and sampling theory.

title: Fourier Uncertainty Principle
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A function and its Fourier transform cannot both be arbitrarily concentrated: the product of their second moments is bounded below.
short: Time and frequency resolutions trade off.
long: Time and frequency resolutions trade off. Gaussians attain equality, centered at the origin after translation and modulation.
proof: Use integration by parts to relate x f to the derivative of f-hat, then apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
consequence: It sets the Gabor limit for time–frequency analysis and quantum bounds.

title: Whittaker–Shannon Sampling Theorem
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A function band-limited to frequencies at most B is determined by samples spaced 1/(2B) apart and reconstructed by sinc interpolation.
short: Band-limited signals have a critical sampling rate.
long: Band-limited signals have a critical sampling rate. Aliasing occurs when the sampling rate falls below twice the bandwidth.
proof: The sampled signal's spectrum is a periodic replication of the original band-limited spectrum; an ideal low-pass filter recovers it.
consequence: It is the mathematical basis of digital audio and imaging.

title: Continuous Wavelet Transform
subject: Signal Processing
statement: The continuous wavelet transform correlates a signal with translated and dilated copies of a mother wavelet, giving a representation with frequency-dependent resolution.
short: Wavelets zoom in on high frequencies and widen for low ones.
long: Wavelets zoom in on high frequencies and widen for low ones. An admissibility condition on the mother wavelet guarantees an inverse transform.
proof: Scaling the wavelet rescales its Fourier transform, giving constant relative bandwidth; a resolution of identity follows from admissibility.
consequence: It provides local regularity analysis, time–frequency plots, and denoising tools.

title: Discrete Cosine Transform and Boundary Symmetry
subject: Signal Processing
statement: The type-II discrete cosine transform equals a Fourier transform of an even extension of the data and is therefore matched to reflecting boundaries.
short: Cosine bases exploit mirror symmetry to avoid boundary jumps.
long: Cosine bases exploit mirror symmetry to avoid boundary jumps. The even extension removes the artificial discontinuity that a periodic extension would create at a block edge.
proof: Extend x evenly to length 2N; the odd sine components cancel in the resulting discrete Fourier transform.
consequence: It is the transform underlying JPEG and MPEG compression.

title: Asymptotic Expansion of the Complementary Error Function
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: For large positive x the complementary error function has a divergent asymptotic expansion in inverse powers of x multiplied by a Gaussian tail.
short: The Gaussian tail controls all algebraic corrections.
long: The Gaussian tail controls all algebraic corrections. Optimal truncation occurs near n about x^2.
proof: Repeated integration by parts in the tail integral of exp(-t^2) generates the series and the remainder.
consequence: It controls tail probabilities and large-deviation approximations.

title: Modified Bessel Functions and Their Asymptotics
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The modified Bessel functions I_nu and K_nu solve the modified Bessel equation; K_nu decays exponentially while I_nu grows exponentially at infinity.
short: One solution grows, the other decays, in modified cylindrical geometry.
long: One solution grows, the other decays, in modified cylindrical geometry. K_nu is the decaying solution used for radial diffusion in unbounded domains.
proof: Reduce the equation with y = x^{-1/2}u and apply steepest descents to the integral representations.
consequence: They appear in heat conduction, radial diffusion, and Bessel processes.

title: Spherical Bessel Functions and Plane Wave Expansion
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: A plane wave expands as a series of spherical Bessel functions multiplied by Legendre polynomials, separating radial and angular dependence.
short: Partial waves decompose a plane wave by angular momentum.
long: Partial waves decompose a plane wave by angular momentum. Large-kr asymptotics of j_l connect the expansion to far-field scattering phases.
proof: Expand in Legendre polynomials and identify the coefficients using the integral representation of j_l.
consequence: It underlies partial-wave analysis of scattering and acoustics.

title: Addition Theorem for Spherical Harmonics
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The sum of squared spherical harmonics of a fixed degree equals a Legendre polynomial of the angle between the two directions.
short: A rotationally invariant kernel depends only on the angle.
long: A rotationally invariant kernel depends only on the angle. The normalisation assumes orthonormal spherical harmonics on the unit sphere.
proof: Both sides are zonal harmonics invariant under rotations about the first direction, and they agree when the directions coincide.
consequence: It reduces pairwise angular interactions to one-dimensional Legendre expansions.

title: Chebyshev Polynomials and the Minimax Property
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Among monic polynomials of degree n, the scaled Chebyshev polynomial has the smallest possible maximum absolute value on the interval from minus one to one.
short: Chebyshev polynomials are optimal uniform approximants.
long: Chebyshev polynomials are optimal uniform approximants. Their extrema equioscillate between plus and minus the minimal value.
proof: If a smaller monic polynomial existed, its difference from the scaled Chebyshev polynomial would have too many zeros to be degree n-1.
consequence: It explains near-optimal Chebyshev interpolation and quadrature nodes.

title: Hermite Polynomials in the Harmonic Oscillator
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Hermite functions are eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, with eigenvalues equally spaced by two.
short: Ladder operators generate the oscillator spectrum.
long: Ladder operators generate the oscillator spectrum. The ground state is Gaussian and each raising operator increases the energy by two in these units.
proof: Apply the creation and annihilation operators to the Gaussian ground state and use their commutation relation.
consequence: It links classical orthogonal polynomials to quantum spectra and Gaussian quadrature.

title: Laplace's Method for Asymptotic Integrals
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: For a large parameter, an integral of exp(-lambda phi) is dominated by the neighbourhood of the nondegenerate minimum of phi and has an explicit Gaussian leading term.
short: The lowest valley carries almost all the mass.
long: The lowest valley carries almost all the mass. Degenerate minima produce different powers of lambda and non-Gaussian profiles.
proof: Expand phi quadratically near its minimum, rescale by lambda to the power minus one half, and apply dominated convergence.
consequence: It gives leading asymptotics of Laplace transforms and partition functions.

title: Saddle-Point Method and Steepest Descent
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: For contour integrals of exp(lambda f), the dominant contributions come from saddle points of f, and the contour can be deformed to paths of steepest descent through them.
short: Complex contours can be steered through the most informative points.
long: Complex contours can be steered through the most informative points. Several saddles may contribute, and their relative weights can change with the argument of lambda.
proof: Use Cauchy's theorem to deform the contour where Im f is constant, then apply Laplace's method along the path.
consequence: It yields coefficient asymptotics and Stirling-type expansions.

title: Method of Stationary Phase
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: An oscillatory integral with a large parameter is dominated by stationary points of the phase, where contributions decay like the inverse square root of the parameter.
short: Rapid oscillations cancel except where the phase pauses.
long: Rapid oscillations cancel except where the phase pauses. Without stationary points the integral decays faster than any power under suitable smoothness assumptions.
proof: Complete the square near each nondegenerate stationary point and evaluate the resulting Fresnel integral by contour rotation.
consequence: It explains decay of oscillatory integrals and yields van der Corput estimates.

title: Watson's Lemma for Laplace Transforms
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The large-parameter expansion of a Laplace transform is obtained term by term from the small-variable expansion of the function being transformed.
short: Local behaviour near zero determines distant Laplace behaviour.
long: Local behaviour near zero determines distant Laplace behaviour. Factorial growth of the coefficients typically makes the resulting series divergent but asymptotic.
proof: Split the integral at a small delta, substitute u=st in the near part, and note the far part is exponentially small.
consequence: It converts Taylor data into large-parameter asymptotics.

title: Stokes Phenomenon and Exponential Asymptotics
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The asymptotic expansion of an analytic function can change across Stokes lines, where exponentially small contributions switch on although the function itself is smooth.
short: Exponentially small terms are hidden from power-series asymptotics until a Stokes line is crossed.
long: Exponentially small terms are hidden from power-series asymptotics until a Stokes line is crossed. Optimal truncation leaves a remainder whose Stokes multiplier varies rapidly across the line.
proof: Track subdominant saddle contributions in steepest-descent representations as the argument of the variable varies.
consequence: It is essential for accurate exponential asymptotics in WKB analysis and resurgence.

title: Borel Summation of Divergent Series
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A factorial-divergent series can often be summed by transforming its coefficients, continuing the transform analytically, and integrating against an exponential kernel.
short: Divide out factorials, then integrate them back in.
long: Divide out factorials, then integrate them back in. The method applies when the Borel transform continues with controlled growth along the integration ray.
proof: Expand the Borel transform and integrate termwise to recover the formal series as an asymptotic expansion.
consequence: It assigns values to many divergent perturbation series in analysing mechanical and quantum systems.

title: Padé Approximants and Analytic Continuation
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A rational Padé approximant matches a prescribed number of Taylor coefficients and often continues the function beyond the radius of convergence of its power series.
short: Rational functions extrapolate where polynomials cannot.
long: Rational functions extrapolate where polynomials cannot. Poles of the approximant often approximate singularities of the underlying function.
proof: Impose the vanishing conditions on the first L+M+1 coefficients and solve the resulting linear system for Q, then define P.
consequence: It accelerates convergence and locates singularities from limited series data.

title: Strict Diagonal Dominance and Iterative Convergence
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: If a matrix is strictly diagonally dominant by rows, both the Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel iterations converge for every initial guess.
short: Dominant diagonals make classical iterations contract.
long: Dominant diagonals make classical iterations contract. The condition is sufficient but not necessary; symmetric positive definiteness is a different sufficient condition for convergence.
proof: Take an eigenvector of the iteration matrix of maximal modulus component and use the dominance inequality to force |lambda| below one.
consequence: It gives a cheap a priori guarantee for large sparse linear solvers.

title: Conjugate Gradient Energy Norm Bound
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For a symmetric positive definite system, conjugate gradient minimizes the energy norm of the error over the Krylov subspace and converges at a rate controlled by the condition number.
short: Conditioning decides how fast conjugate gradient converges.
long: Conditioning decides how fast conjugate gradient converges. The bound is pessimistic in the presence of favourable eigenvalue clustering.
proof: Use the Galerkin optimality of the iterate and a Chebyshev polynomial small on the spectrum and equal to one at zero.
consequence: It quantifies why preconditioning matters.

title: Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Applying a symmetric positive definite preconditioner changes the convergence bound of conjugate gradient by replacing the original condition number with that of the preconditioned matrix.
short: A good preconditioner clusters the spectrum.
long: A good preconditioner clusters the spectrum. Common choices include incomplete factorisations, multigrid, and domain decomposition.
proof: Preconditioned conjugate gradient is conjugate gradient in the M-inner product, so the spectral bound applies to M^{-1}A.
consequence: It makes large sparse systems solvable in far fewer iterations.

title: Arnoldi Iteration and Hessenberg Reduction
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The Arnoldi iteration builds an orthonormal Krylov basis together with an upper Hessenberg matrix representing the compressed action of A.
short: Orthogonalise successive matrix-vector products.
long: Orthogonalise successive matrix-vector products. The small Hessenberg matrix provides eigenvalue estimates called Ritz values.
proof: Apply modified Gram–Schmidt to Aq_k after the previous basis vectors; only the last m+1 terms can survive.
consequence: It underlies GMRES and Krylov eigenvalue solvers.

title: Lanczos Algorithm and Tridiagonalisation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For Hermitian matrices the Arnoldi relation collapses to a three-term recurrence generating a symmetric tridiagonal matrix.
short: Hermitian symmetry reduces the Krylov work to three terms.
long: Hermitian symmetry reduces the Krylov work to three terms. The diagonal and subdiagonal entries of T_m are the recurrence coefficients.
proof: Orthogonality of the residuals forces all Hessenberg entries beyond the first subdiagonal to vanish.
consequence: It gives efficient extreme eigenvalue estimates and moment approximations.

title: Power Method and Dominant Eigenvalue
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: If a matrix has a unique dominant eigenvalue, repeated multiplication by the matrix converges to a corresponding eigenvector at a rate set by the ratio of the two largest eigenvalue moduli.
short: Repeated multiplication amplifies the dominant direction.
long: Repeated multiplication amplifies the dominant direction. Complex dominant eigenvalues produce rotation rather than convergence of the direction.
proof: Expand the initial vector in an eigenbasis and observe that normalisation removes the dominant scalar factor.
consequence: It is the simplest eigenvalue algorithm and an ancestor of link-analysis computations.

title: Inverse Iteration and Rayleigh Quotient Shift
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Applying the power method to the inverse of A minus a shift converges to the eigenvector whose eigenvalue is closest to the shift.
short: Inversion turns the nearest eigenvalue into the dominant one.
long: Inversion turns the nearest eigenvalue into the dominant one. Updating the shift to the current Rayleigh quotient gives rapid local convergence.
proof: Eigenvalues of the inverse matrix are (lambda_i - sigma)^{-1}, so the closest eigenvalue has the largest modulus.
consequence: It computes a single eigenvector accurately from an eigenvalue estimate.

title: Rayleigh Quotient Bounds for Hermitian Matrices
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The Rayleigh quotient of a Hermitian matrix lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues, and its stationary points are exactly the eigenvectors.
short: Eigenvalues are the extreme averages of the quadratic form.
long: Eigenvalues are the extreme averages of the quadratic form. The min–max principle refines this to characterise every eigenvalue by a subspace dimension.
proof: Diagonalise A by a unitary matrix; the quotient becomes a weighted average of the eigenvalues.
consequence: It supports variational eigenvalue estimates and optimisation methods.

title: Bauer–Fike Eigenvalue Perturbation Bound
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For a diagonalisable matrix, every eigenvalue of a perturbed matrix lies within the condition number of the eigenvector matrix times the perturbation norm of some original eigenvalue.
short: Non-normal eigenvector bases amplify eigenvalue perturbations.
long: Non-normal eigenvector bases amplify eigenvalue perturbations. For normal matrices the condition number equals one and eigenvalues are perfectly stable.
proof: Let v be an eigenvector of A+E, expand S^{-1}v, and apply the triangle inequality to (Lambda + S^{-1}ES)y = mu y.
consequence: It explains the sensitivity of eigenvalues of highly non-normal matrices.

title: Weyl Inequality for Hermitian Eigenvalues
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Perturbing a Hermitian matrix in spectral norm moves each ordered eigenvalue by at most the perturbation norm.
short: Hermitian eigenvalues are Lipschitz functions of the matrix.
long: Hermitian eigenvalues are Lipschitz functions of the matrix. The statement fails for non-Hermitian matrices without the eigenvector condition number.
proof: Apply the Courant–Fischer min–max principle to quadratic forms differing by at most the norm of E.
consequence: It gives rigorous eigenvalue stability in numerical linear algebra.

title: Davis–Kahan Subspace Perturbation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: If an eigenvalue cluster is separated from the rest of the spectrum by a gap, a small Hermitian perturbation moves the corresponding invariant subspace by an amount proportional to the perturbation divided by the gap.
short: Spectral gaps protect invariant subspaces.
long: Spectral gaps protect invariant subspaces. The bound degrades as clusters merge, reflecting genuine eigenvector ambiguity.
proof: Write the subspace rotation as the solution of a Sylvester equation and bound it using the spectral separation.
consequence: It justifies eigenvector stability claims in spectral clustering and perturbation theory.

title: Eckart–Young Low-Rank Approximation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Truncating the singular value decomposition after k terms gives the best rank-k approximation in both the Frobenius and spectral norms.
short: The largest singular values carry the optimal low-rank structure.
long: The largest singular values carry the optimal low-rank structure. The truncated SVD also gives the best approximation in any unitarily invariant norm.
proof: Use the min–max characterisation of singular values or the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem.
consequence: It underpins principal component analysis, image compression, and model reduction.

title: Pseudospectra and Nonnormal Sensitivity
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The epsilon-pseudospectrum of a matrix is the set of complex numbers that are eigenvalues of some perturbation of norm at most epsilon, and it can be far larger than the spectrum for nonnormal matrices.
short: Spectra can be misleading when eigenvectors are nearly dependent.
long: Spectra can be misleading when eigenvectors are nearly dependent. Transient growth of solutions of x'=Ax is governed by pseudospectral geometry rather than eigenvalues alone.
proof: Use the resolvent characterisation and perturbation of a nearly eigenvector basis to construct an eigenvalue of a nearby matrix.
consequence: It explains transient instability in fluid and control systems.

title: Thomas Algorithm for Tridiagonal Systems
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: A tridiagonal linear system can be solved in time linear in its dimension by a specialised elimination without pivoting when diagonal dominance holds.
short: Sparse band structure makes Gaussian elimination cheap.
long: Sparse band structure makes Gaussian elimination cheap. The algorithm is Gaussian elimination with the zeros outside the band skipped automatically.
proof: Eliminate one variable at a time; only the neighbour coefficient changes at each step.
consequence: It solves one-dimensional finite-difference systems with minimal work.

title: Iterative Refinement of Linear Solutions
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Computing the residual of an approximate solution and solving for a correction can improve forward accuracy when the residual is computed in higher precision.
short: A cheap correction step recovers digits lost in factorisation.
long: A cheap correction step recovers digits lost in factorisation. The method is most effective when the residual benefits from extended precision arithmetic.
proof: The error e = x - x-hat satisfies A e = r exactly; solving approximately reduces the error by the solve accuracy.
consequence: It improves solution quality with little extra storage.

title: Restricted Isometry Property and Sparse Recovery
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: If a measurement matrix approximately preserves the Euclidean norm of all sufficiently sparse vectors, then l1 minimisation recovers those sparse vectors from few linear measurements.
short: Norm preservation on sparse vectors makes compression lossless.
long: Norm preservation on sparse vectors makes compression lossless. Random matrices satisfy the restricted isometry property with high probability at near-optimal measurement rates.
proof: Compare the cones of feasible sparse errors and use the restricted isometry inequalities plus the null-space condition.
consequence: It justifies compressed sensing in imaging and signal acquisition.

title: Galerkin Finite Element Discretisation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: A Galerkin finite element method seeks an approximate solution in a piecewise polynomial space by requiring the residual to be orthogonal to that space.
short: Approximate in a local basis and enforce the weak form exactly.
long: Approximate in a local basis and enforce the weak form exactly. Local support of basis functions yields sparse stiffness matrices.
proof: Multiply by a test function, integrate by parts to get the weak formulation, restrict both spaces to V_h, and solve the resulting linear system.
consequence: It handles complex geometries and is a standard tool in engineering simulation.

title: Lax Equivalence Theorem
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For a consistent finite-difference approximation to a well-posed linear initial value problem, stability is necessary and sufficient for convergence.
short: Stable and consistent schemes converge.
long: Stable and consistent schemes converge. The result is the numerical analogue of the fundamental theorem of linear approximations.
proof: Split the global error into local truncation error propagated by powers of the stable amplification operator and sum the contributions.
consequence: It structures the analysis of time-stepping methods for PDEs.

title: Von Neumann Fourier Stability Analysis
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For a linear constant-coefficient scheme on a uniform grid, stability is checked by inserting Fourier modes and requiring the amplification factor to be bounded by one plus a constant times the time step.
short: Fourier modes reveal whether a scheme amplifies errors.
long: Fourier modes reveal whether a scheme amplifies errors. The criterion is necessary for periodic problems and sufficient in many constant-coefficient settings.
proof: Substitute the mode into the stencil and analyse the resulting amplification symbol over all wave numbers.
consequence: It gives quick stability restrictions such as Courant limits for explicit schemes.

title: Upwind Scheme for Linear Advection
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: An upwind finite-difference scheme for linear advection uses the difference taken against the flow direction, giving a stable but only first-order accurate method with numerical diffusion.
short: Look upstream for information carried by the flow.
long: Look upstream for information carried by the flow. The scheme is monotone and satisfies a discrete maximum principle under the Courant condition.
proof: A Fourier mode analysis gives amplification factor modulus at most one when a delta t over delta x is at most one.
consequence: It is the simplest stable discretisation of transport and a building block of CFD.

title: Godunov's Method for Conservation Laws
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Godunov's method evolves cell averages by solving exact or approximate Riemann problems at cell interfaces and averaging the resulting solution.
short: Resolve shocks locally, then average.
long: Resolve shocks locally, then average. Higher-order extensions use reconstruction and limiters to avoid spurious oscillations.
proof: Integrate the conservation law over a cell and use the divergence theorem; the interface flux comes from the Riemann solution.
consequence: It is the foundation of modern shock-capturing schemes.

title: Entropy Condition and Lax Shock Condition
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Weak solutions of nonlinear conservation laws are not unique; the Lax entropy condition selects the physically admissible shock by requiring characteristics to enter the shock.
short: Shocks must swallow characteristics, not emit them.
long: Shocks must swallow characteristics, not emit them. For convex flux this is equivalent to an entropy inequality for a suitable convex entropy function.
proof: Compare characteristic speeds on either side with the Rankine–Hugoniot shock speed.
consequence: It restores uniqueness and matches the vanishing-viscosity limit.

title: Finite Volume Conservative Discretisation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Finite volume methods update cell averages using fluxes across cell faces, so the discrete scheme conserves the quantity exactly.
short: What leaves one cell enters the next.
long: What leaves one cell enters the next. Conservation is essential for computing correct shock speeds.
proof: Integrate the conservation law over each control volume and apply the divergence theorem to convert volume integrals to face fluxes.
consequence: It is the standard framework for compressible flow and hyperbolic PDE solvers.

title: Spectral Methods and Exponential Convergence
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Expanding a smooth solution in global orthogonal polynomials or trigonometric functions gives errors that decay faster than any algebraic power, often exponentially.
short: Global bases exploit smoothness for spectacular accuracy.
long: Global bases exploit smoothness for spectacular accuracy. Accuracy degrades for discontinuous solutions, motivating filtering and local reconstructions.
proof: Estimate the tail of the orthogonal expansion using analyticity and contour deformation of the coefficient integrals.
consequence: They are highly effective in smooth problems such as turbulence direct simulation and wave propagation.

title: Richardson Extrapolation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Combining approximations computed at two different step sizes can cancel the leading error term and raise the order of accuracy.
short: Two imperfect answers can be combined into a better one.
long: Two imperfect answers can be combined into a better one. Repeating the elimination using a hierarchy of step sizes gives Romberg integration.
proof: Insert the assumed error expansions for h and h/2 and choose coefficients that cancel the h^p term.
consequence: It boosts accuracy cheaply without changing the underlying scheme.

title: Implicit Euler Method for Stiff Equations
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The backward Euler method evaluates the right-hand side at the new time step, giving first-order accuracy but unconditional stability for dissipative linear problems.
short: Solve implicitly to survive stiff modes.
long: Solve implicitly to survive stiff modes. Each step requires solving a nonlinear or linear system, often by Newton's method.
proof: For the scalar test equation y'=lambda y with Re lambda<0, the amplification factor 1/(1-lambda dt) has modulus below one for all positive step sizes.
consequence: It is a robust default for stiff ODEs and diffusion equations.

title: Implicit Trapezoidal Rule for ODEs
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The trapezoidal rule for ordinary differential equations averages the right-hand side at the old and new time levels, giving second-order accuracy and A-stability.
short: Average the slope at both ends of the step.
long: Average the slope at both ends of the step. It is equivalent to the implicit midpoint rule up to a coordinate transformation for linear problems.
proof: Taylor expansion gives second order; for y'=lambda y the amplification factor (1+z/2)/(1-z/2) has modulus at most one when Re z is nonpositive.
consequence: It combines good stability with useful accuracy for moderately stiff problems.

title: Symplectic Integrators and Long-Time Energy Behaviour
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: A symplectic integrator preserves the symplectic two-form of a Hamiltonian system and therefore keeps a modified Hamiltonian nearly constant over very long times.
short: Preserve geometry and the energy error stays bounded.
long: Preserve geometry and the energy error stays bounded. The numerical solution follows the exact flow of a nearby Hamiltonian, not the original one.
proof: Check that the method's update map has symplectic Jacobian; backward error analysis then constructs the modified Hamiltonian.
consequence: They are the methods of choice for celestial mechanics and molecular dynamics.

title: Velocity Verlet Integration
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Velocity Verlet updates positions, forces, and velocities in a symmetric splitting that is symplectic and second-order accurate for mechanical systems.
latex: x_{n+1}=x_n+v_n\Delta t+\tfrac12 a_n\Delta t^2,\quad v_{n+1}=v_n+\tfrac12(a_n+a_{n+1})\Delta t
short: A half-step force, a full-step position, another half-step force.
long: A half-step force, a full-step position, another half-step force. It requires one force evaluation per step when forces are cached between steps.
proof: The update is the composition of exact flows for the kinetic and potential parts, which is symmetric and symplectic.
consequence: It is the standard integrator in molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Runge–Kutta Order Conditions
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The coefficients of a Runge–Kutta method must satisfy algebraic order conditions obtained by matching Taylor expansions of the exact and numerical flows; explicit s-stage methods cannot attain order greater than s.
short: Order is encoded in polynomial identities among stage weights.
long: Order is encoded in polynomial identities among stage weights. The full set of conditions is indexed by rooted trees in the Butcher theory.
proof: Expand the exact solution and the stage values in Taylor series and equate coefficients of elementary differentials.
consequence: It guides the design of high-order methods and proves stage-order barriers.

title: Dahlquist Barrier for Linear Multistep Methods
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: An A-stable linear multistep method has order at most two, and among explicit linear multistep methods the order cannot exceed two.
short: There is no high-order A-stable linear multistep method.
long: There is no high-order A-stable linear multistep method. The second-order trapezoidal rule attains the barrier for implicit methods.
proof: Study the roots of the characteristic polynomial on the negative real axis and apply the root condition plus order conditions.
consequence: It motivated the development of Runge–Kutta and rational approximations for stiff problems.

title: Exponential Integrators for Semilinear Problems
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For equations whose linear part dominates, exponential integrators treat that part exactly via the matrix exponential and integrate only the remaining nonlinearity.
short: Integrate the stiff linear part exactly.
long: Integrate the stiff linear part exactly. Approximations of the phi-functions of L determine the practical scheme and its order.
proof: Apply the variation-of-constants formula over one time step and approximate the nonlinear integral.
consequence: They are effective for stiff PDEs and semi-discretised parabolic problems.

title: Adaptive Quadrature and Error Estimates
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Comparing a quadrature estimate with a finer or higher-order estimate provides a local error indicator that can drive recursive interval subdivision.
short: Spend evaluations where the integrand is hard.
long: Spend evaluations where the integrand is hard. Gauss–Kronrod pairs reuse function values to obtain the estimate cheaply.
proof: Under a smooth error expansion the difference of the two estimates behaves like a known power of the interval length.
consequence: It makes automatic integration reliable for functions with localised difficulty.

title: First-Order Convexity Inequality
subject: Optimization
statement: A differentiable function is convex on a convex domain precisely when its graph lies above every tangent hyperplane.
short: Tangents support a convex graph from below.
long: Tangents support a convex graph from below. A strong convexity version adds a quadratic term with coefficient mu.
proof: For convex f use convexity of one-dimensional restrictions and let the step tend to zero; conversely the inequality implies midpoint convexity and continuity.
consequence: It gives global optimality certificates and lower bounds in optimisation algorithms.

title: Fenchel Conjugate and Biconjugacy
subject: Optimization
statement: The Fenchel conjugate of a proper convex function is convex and lower semicontinuous, and taking the conjugate twice returns the closed convex envelope.
short: Conjugacy exchanges a function with its family of supporting hyperplanes.
long: Conjugacy exchanges a function with its family of supporting hyperplanes. Affine functions are fixed points only in the appropriate closure sense.
proof: Use the Fenchel–Young inequality and the separation theorem to identify the biconjugate.
consequence: It provides the duality dictionary for convex optimisation.

title: Moreau Envelope and Proximal Mapping
subject: Optimization
statement: The Moreau envelope smooths a proper lower semicontinuous convex function by quadratic regularisation, and the minimiser defines its proximal mapping.
short: Add a quadratic well and take the value at its bottom.
long: Add a quadratic well and take the value at its bottom. The envelope is continuously differentiable with gradient (x - proxlambda f(x))/lambda.
proof: Strong convexity of the added quadratic gives a unique minimiser; the envelope theorem gives the gradient formula.
consequence: It unify handles nonsmooth objectives in proximal algorithms.

title: Proximal Point Algorithm Convergence
subject: Optimization
statement: Iterating the proximal mapping of a proper closed convex function with positive step sizes converges to a minimiser whenever one exists.
short: Repeated proximal steps descend toward a minimiser.
long: Repeated proximal steps descend toward a minimiser. The iteration is firmly nonexpansive, which yields Fejér monotonicity to the solution set.
proof: Use the optimality condition to show the distance to any minimiser decreases, then establish asymptotic regularity.
consequence: It underlies proximal gradient and splitting methods for nonsmooth problems.

title: Frank–Wolfe Conditional Gradient Method
subject: Optimization
statement: For smooth convex minimisation over a compact convex set, conditional gradient steps minimise a linearisation of the objective over the feasible set, avoiding projected steps.
short: Move toward the best vertex of the linear model.
long: Move toward the best vertex of the linear model. The sublinear convergence rate is O(1/k) and improves under curvature assumptions.
proof: Convexity bounds the objective gap by a linearised gap; descent in the linear minimum over the compact set gives the rate.
consequence: It is attractive for large-scale constraints where projection is expensive.

title: Levenberg–Marquardt Algorithm
subject: Optimization
statement: Nonlinear least squares can be solved by interpolating between Gauss–Newton steps and gradient descent through a damped normal-equation system.
short: Damping regularises Gauss–Newton when the Jacobian is ill-conditioned.
long: Damping regularises Gauss–Newton when the Jacobian is ill-conditioned. Increasing lambda shortens the step and makes it a gradient-descent direction; decreasing it recovers fast local convergence.
proof: The damping term makes the coefficient matrix positive definite, giving a descent direction for the sum of squared residuals.
consequence: It is a standard curve-fitting tool in scientific computing.

title: Primal–Dual Interior-Point Methods
subject: Optimization
statement: Primal–dual interior-point methods follow a central path of perturbed complementarity conditions while reducing a barrier parameter toward zero.
short: Track approximate solutions from the interior to the boundary.
long: Track approximate solutions from the interior to the boundary. Newton's method solves the perturbed KKT system at each barrier parameter value.
proof: Strict convexity and Slater's condition give a unique central path converging to an optimal primal–dual pair.
consequence: They solve large linear and convex programs in a polynomial number of iterations in practice and theory.

title: Logarithmic Barrier and the Central Path
subject: Optimization
statement: Adding a logarithmic barrier for inequality constraints creates a smooth subproblem whose minimisers form the central path approaching the constrained optimum as the barrier weight vanishes.
short: The barrier keeps iterates away from the boundary until convergence.
long: The barrier keeps iterates away from the boundary until convergence. The distance to the boundary is at most the number of constraints divided by t at a central-point solution.
proof: The barrier tends to infinity at the boundary; first-order optimality gives perturbed complementarity conditions.
consequence: It underlies polynomial-time convex optimisation algorithms.

title: Subgradient Method for Nonsmooth Convex Functions
subject: Optimization
statement: For a convex but nondifferentiable function, moving in the direction of a negative subgradient with suitably diminishing step sizes converges to a minimiser.
short: Any supporting hyperplane gives a usable descent direction.
long: Any supporting hyperplane gives a usable descent direction. Unlike gradient descent the objective need not decrease at every step.
proof: Use the subgradient inequality to bound the squared distance to the optimum and sum the resulting inequalities.
consequence: It handles nonsmooth objectives such as l1 penalties and max-functions.

title: Mirror Descent and Bregman Divergence
subject: Optimization
statement: Mirror descent replaces the Euclidean proximity term by a Bregman divergence, adapting the algorithm to the geometry of the feasible set.
short: Use a distance shaped for the problem's geometry.
long: Use a distance shaped for the problem's geometry. Euclidean geometry recovers projected subgradient descent; entropy geometry gives multiplicative weights.
proof: The three-point identity for Bregman divergences replaces the Pythagorean identity of Euclidean projections in the rate analysis.
consequence: It yields dimension-dependent but geometry-optimal rates for high-dimensional problems.

title: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers
subject: Optimization
statement: ADMM splits a convex objective across variables linked by a linear constraint and alternates minimisation steps with a dual variable update.
short: Solve small subproblems and communicate through a dual price.
long: Solve small subproblems and communicate through a dual price. It converges for proper closed convex objectives under mild conditions, with linear rates under strong convexity.
proof: Show monotone decrease of an augmented Lagrangian-based Lyapunov function and primal–dual residual convergence.
consequence: It is widely used in distributed optimisation and signal processing.

title: Farkas' Lemma and Certificates of Infeasibility
subject: Optimization
statement: A linear system has no nonnegative solution exactly when there exists a vector certifying infeasibility by a nonnegative linear combination of the constraints.
short: Infeasibility has an explicit algebraic witness.
long: Infeasibility has an explicit algebraic witness. Equivalent forms yield strong duality for linear programming.
proof: Separate the closed convex cone generated by the columns of A from the point b.
consequence: It underpins LP duality solvers and infeasibility certificates.

title: von Neumann Minimax Theorem
subject: Optimization
statement: For a continuous function convex in one variable and concave in the other on compact convex sets, the minimum over one variable of the maximum over the other equals the maximum over the other of the minimum.
short: Under convexity the order of play does not change the value.
long: Under convexity the order of play does not change the value. Compactness can be relaxed to coercivity in many applications.
proof: Use a separating hyperplane on the set of functions above the concave envelope, or apply Kakutani's fixed-point theorem.
consequence: It is the foundation of zero-sum game theory and convex duality.

title: Envelope Theorem for Parametric Optimisation
subject: Optimization
statement: The derivative of the optimal value of a smooth constrained optimisation problem with respect to a parameter equals the partial derivative of the Lagrangian at the optimal solution.
short: Indirect effects through the optimiser vanish at the optimum.
long: Indirect effects through the optimiser vanish at the optimum. This follows from the envelope condition and the first-order optimality of the inner problem.
proof: Differentiate the value function and use stationarity of the Lagrangian with respect to the decision variables.
consequence: It gives comparative statics in economics and sensitivity information in design.

title: Danskin's Theorem on Directional Derivatives
subject: Optimization
statement: The directional derivative of a maximum of smoothly parameterised functions equals the maximum of the directional derivatives over the active maximisers.
short: Only the currently best alternatives matter locally.
long: Only the currently best alternatives matter locally. Compactness of Y and smoothness of f give existence and formula validity.
proof: Use uniform convergence of difference quotients on the compact active set.
consequence: It computes gradients of max-functions and robust objective values.

title: Nash Equilibrium Existence in Finite Games
subject: Game Theory
statement: Every finite game with mixed strategies has at least one Nash equilibrium.
short: Randomisation guarantees that some stable strategy profile exists.
long: Randomisation guarantees that some stable strategy profile exists. Equilibria may be multiple and may involve strictly dominated strategies in special cases.
proof: Apply Kakutani's fixed-point theorem to the best-response correspondence, which is nonempty, convex-valued, and upper hemicontinuous.
consequence: It is the central existence result of noncooperative game theory.

title: Prisoner's Dilemma and Dominant Strategies
subject: Game Theory
statement: In the prisoner's dilemma each player has a strictly dominant strategy to defect, so the unique equilibrium is Pareto dominated by mutual cooperation.
short: Individual rationality can destroy collective optimality.
long: Individual rationality can destroy collective optimality. Repeated interaction can sustain cooperation through the folk theorem.
proof: Defection strictly dominates cooperation for each player regardless of the opponent, so the unique equilibrium is mutual defection.
consequence: It models overfishing, arms races, and price wars.

title: Backward Induction in Finite Extensive Games
subject: Game Theory
statement: In a finite game of perfect information, optimal choices can be computed by working backwards from terminal nodes, one information set at a time.
short: Solve the last move first and roll forward.
long: Solve the last move first and roll forward. Zermelo's theorem follows: finite deterministic zero-sum games of perfect information are determined.
proof: Induct on the height of the game tree; each player's optimal continuation at a node determines the subtree value.
consequence: It computes subgame perfect outcomes in chess-like settings and bargaining models.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
subject: Game Theory
statement: A strategy profile is subgame perfect if its restriction to every subgame is a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.
short: Threats must be credible at every stage.
long: Threats must be credible at every stage. Backward induction finds all subgame perfect equilibria in finite perfect-information games.
proof: Verify equilibrium conditions recursively starting from terminal subgames.
consequence: It refines Nash equilibrium by eliminating noncredible behaviour.

title: Folk Theorem for Repeated Games
subject: Game Theory
statement: In an indefinitely repeated game with sufficiently patient players, any feasible and individually rational payoff profile can be sustained as a subgame perfect equilibrium.
short: The shadow of the future supports cooperation.
long: The shadow of the future supports cooperation. Grim-trigger strategies punish deviation by reverting to a minmax punishment forever.
proof: Construct trigger strategies, check one-shot deviation incentives, and use patience to make discounted future losses dominate current gains.
consequence: It explains collusion, reciprocity, and cooperation without external enforcement.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
subject: Game Theory
statement: In a game with incomplete information, a Bayesian Nash equilibrium assigns each type of each player a strategy maximising expected utility given beliefs about other types and their strategies.
short: Strategy maps types into actions and optimises on average.
long: Strategy maps types into actions and optimises on average. It generalises Nash equilibrium to settings where payoff-relevant information is private.
proof: Apply a fixed-point argument to the product of best-response correspondences over type-contingent strategies.
consequence: It models auctions, signalling, and asymmetric-information markets.

title: Spence Signalling Model and Separating Equilibria
subject: Game Theory
statement: When education is more costly for low-ability workers, a sufficiently high level can separate types: high-ability workers choose it and low-ability workers do not.
short: A costly signal can reveal private information.
long: A costly signal can reveal private information. Pooling equilibria may also exist when the single-crossing condition fails.
proof: Impose incentive compatibility for each type and use the single-crossing property of cost curves to find a separating threshold.
consequence: It founded the economics of asymmetric information and credential markets.

title: Revenue Equivalence Theorem
subject: Game Theory
statement: In symmetric independent-private-value auctions, any mechanism that allocates efficiently to the highest bidder and gives the lowest type zero expected utility yields the same expected revenue.
short: Allocation and the lowest payoff determine revenue.
long: Allocation and the lowest payoff determine revenue. The revenue depends only on the allocation rule, not on the payment format.
proof: Use the envelope theorem on the expected utility of each type and integrate the virtual-value expression.
consequence: It unifies the analysis of first-price, second-price, and other standard auctions.

title: Vickrey Second-Price Auction
subject: Game Theory
statement: In a sealed-bid second-price auction with private values, bidding one's true valuation is a weakly dominant strategy and the winner pays the second-highest bid.
short: You pay the other bid, not your own.
long: You pay the other bid, not your own. Truthful bidding remains optimal even when bidders are risk neutral and values are independent.
proof: Compare payoff under truthful bidding with any deviation in the cases where the highest competing bid is above or below the valuation.
consequence: It is a benchmark for implementing efficient allocations.

title: Myerson Optimal Auction and Virtual Valuation
subject: Game Theory
statement: For a single item with independent bidders, the revenue-maximising mechanism allocates to the bidder with the largest virtual valuation, provided it is positive, and charges the threshold bid.
short: Optimise over virtual values rather than bids.
long: Optimise over virtual values rather than bids. Regular distributions have monotone virtual valuations, so the optimal mechanism is a reserve-price auction.
proof: Write expected revenue as the expectation of virtual surplus and pointwise maximise it subject to monotonicity.
consequence: It launched modern auction theory and optimal mechanism design.

title: Vickrey–Clarke–Groves Mechanism
subject: Game Theory
statement: The VCG mechanism chooses an allocation maximising reported total value and charges each agent the externality they impose on others, making truthful reporting dominant.
short: Pay the harm you cause to everyone else.
long: Pay the harm you cause to everyone else. It generalises the second-price auction to arbitrary allocation problems.
proof: An agent's utility including the payment equals total reported welfare plus a term independent of their own report, so maximising total value is dominant.
consequence: It implements efficient outcomes in public goods and combinatorial auctions.

title: Revelation Principle for Direct Mechanisms
subject: Game Theory
statement: Any equilibrium outcome of an arbitrary mechanism can be replicated by a direct mechanism in which agents truthfully report their types.
latex: \text{any implementable outcome}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{implementable by truthful direct mechanism}
short: Focus on truthful mechanisms without losing generality.
long: Focus on truthful mechanisms without losing generality. The direct mechanism asks for types and mimics the equilibrium strategies of the original game.
proof: Construct the direct rule that maps reported types to the equilibrium outcome of the original mechanism; truthfulness follows from the original equilibrium conditions.
consequence: It reduces mechanism design to designing incentive-compatible direct rules.

title: Median Voter Theorem
subject: Game Theory
statement: In majority voting over a single policy with voters having single-peaked preferences, the policy preferred by the median voter is a Condorcet winner.
latex: \text{median ideal point }m^*\ \text{defeats any other policy in a pairwise vote}
short: Elections converge to the middle of the distribution.
long: Elections converge to the middle of the distribution. The conclusion can fail with multidimensional policy spaces or non-single-peaked preferences.
proof: Any policy on one side of the median is defeated by the median point because a majority lies closer to the median.
consequence: It explains policy convergence and centrist platforms.

title: Cournot Duopoly Equilibrium
subject: Game Theory
statement: When firms compete by choosing quantities with a linear inverse demand curve, the unique Nash equilibrium has each firm producing one third of the competitive output.
short: Output competition yields prices above marginal cost.
long: Output competition yields prices above marginal cost. As the number of firms grows, Cournot output approaches the competitive outcome.
proof: Solve each firm's profit-maximisation problem for its best response and intersect the two reaction curves.
consequence: It is the standard benchmark for oligopoly analysis.

title: Bertrand Price Competition
subject: Game Theory
statement: With homogeneous products and constant marginal cost, price competition between two firms drives the equilibrium price down to marginal cost.
short: A small undercut captures the whole market.
long: A small undercut captures the whole market. Capacity constraints or product differentiation soften the result.
proof: If both prices exceed cost, either firm gains by slightly undercutting; no price below cost can be optimal.
consequence: It highlights how the strategic variable changes market outcomes.

title: Walrasian Equilibrium and Market Clearing
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: A Walrasian equilibrium consists of prices and allocations such that every agent maximises utility subject to their budget and all markets clear.
short: One price vector makes every plan compatible.
long: One price vector makes every plan compatible. Prices are only defined up to a common positive scalar, reflecting homogeneity.
proof: Given optimising demands and supplies, Walras' law implies that clearing all but one market clearing implies the last clears.
consequence: It is the central solution concept of general equilibrium theory.

title: Arrow–Debreu Existence of General Equilibrium
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: An exchange or production economy with convex preferences, convex production sets, and suitable boundedness has at least one competitive equilibrium.
short: Convexity and continuity guarantee a market-clearing price vector.
