long: Convexity and continuity guarantee a market-clearing price vector. The proof relies on fixed-point theorems applied to an excess-demand correspondence.
proof: Normalise prices to the simplex, apply Kakutani's theorem to a truncated excess-demand map, and show the limiting allocation clears markets.
consequence: It provides a rigorous foundation for Adam Smith's invisible hand intuition.

title: First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: Every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient under local nonsatiation of preferences.
short: Markets leave no mutually beneficial trades unexploited.
long: Markets leave no mutually beneficial trades unexploited. It requires complete markets and no externalities or public goods.
proof: If an allocation Pareto dominated it, the budget inequalities and local nonsatiation would imply an impossible inequality after multiplying by equilibrium prices.
consequence: It gives a formal case for market efficiency under ideal conditions.

title: Second Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: Under convexity assumptions, any Pareto efficient allocation can be supported as a competitive equilibrium after a suitable redistribution of initial endowments.
short: Equity and efficiency can be separated in principle.
long: Equity and efficiency can be separated in principle. The required transfers are lump-sum and depend on the desired allocation.
proof: Separate the preferred allocation from the aggregate production set and choose endowments so the resulting budget hyperplane supports it.
consequence: It underpins the theory of redistribution without distorting prices.

title: Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: If a chosen bundle was affordable when another bundle was chosen, the second bundle cannot be affordable when the first is chosen unless choices are identical.
short: Observed choices cannot contradict themselves.
long: Observed choices cannot contradict themselves. The strong axiom extends the condition to chains of revealed preference.
proof: Assume both bundles were chosen in the two budget situations and derive a contradiction from the maximisation hypothesis.
consequence: It tests whether demand data are consistent with utility maximisation.

title: Slutsky Equation for Demand
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: The change in Marshallian demand caused by a price change decomposes into a substitution effect and an income effect.
latex: \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}=\frac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_j}-\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial m}x_j
short: Price changes shift both relative attractiveness and purchasing power.
long: Price changes shift both relative attractiveness and purchasing power. The substitution effect is negative semidefinite for the Hicksian demand.
proof: Differentiate the identity h(p,u(p,m)) = x(p,m) with respect to p_j using the envelope theorem.
consequence: It explains Giffen goods and the shape of demand curves.

title: Euler Equation of Optimal Consumption
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: In intertemporal consumption choice, the marginal utility of consuming today equals the discounted expected marginal utility of consuming tomorrow times the gross return on savings.
short: Consumers equalise the marginal value of saving and spending.
long: Consumers equalise the marginal value of saving and spending. Log utility with beta times the return less than one implies declining consumption when the return is high.
proof: Set up the Lagrangian for the two-period budget and differentiate with respect to current consumption.
consequence: It is the workhorse condition of growth and asset-pricing models.

title: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans Growth Model
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: In the neoclassical growth model with optimising households, the economy converges to a steady-state capital stock where the modified golden-rule condition holds.
latex: \dot k=f(k)-c-(n+\delta)k,\qquad f'(k^*)=\rho+n+\delta\ \text{at the modified golden rule}
short: Saving, depreciation, and population growth balance in the long run.
long: Saving, depreciation, and population growth balance in the long run. The discount rate makes steady-state capital lower than the golden-rule level when rho is positive.
proof: Solve the Hamiltonian system in (k,c), linearise around the steady state, and apply the transversality condition.
consequence: It explains long-run growth and capital accumulation without exogenous saving behaviour.

title: Black–Scholes Option Pricing Formula
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: Under constant volatility and risk-free rate with no dividends, the price of a European call is given by a closed formula involving the standard normal distribution function.
short: Dynamic hedging removes risk and fixes the option price.
long: Dynamic hedging removes risk and fixes the option price. The formula assumes frictionless markets and continuous trading.
proof: Apply Itô's lemma to the option price and choose a delta-hedging portfolio whose drift equals the risk-free rate.
consequence: It founded modern derivatives pricing and risk management.

title: Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: A market has no arbitrage essentially if and only if there exists an equivalent martingale measure under which discounted asset prices are martingales.
latex: \text{no arbitrage}\iff \exists\ \mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P:\ e^{-rt}S_t\ \text{is a }\mathbb Q\text{-martingale}
short: Arbitrage-free prices are expectations under a risk-neutral measure.
long: Arbitrage-free prices are expectations under a risk-neutral measure. In incomplete markets the equivalent martingale measure need not be unique.
proof: Use the Hahn–Banach or separating hyperplane theorem to construct the pricing functional and show it defines a positive measure.
consequence: It links derivative pricing to martingale theory and completeness.

title: Put–Call Parity
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: For European options with the same strike and maturity and no dividends, the call price minus the put price equals the spot price minus the discounted strike.
short: A long call and short put replicate the underlying financed by borrowing.
long: A long call and short put replicate the underlying financed by borrowing. Dividends or foreign-currency carry modify the right-hand side by the present value of the dividend stream.
proof: At maturity both portfolios pay max(S_T-K,0)-max(K-S_T,0)=S_T-K; no-arbitrage then forces equality of initial values.
consequence: It detects arbitrage violations and links call and put markets.

title: Kalman Controllability Rank Condition
subject: Control Theory
statement: A finite-dimensional linear system is controllable exactly when the matrix formed from B, AB, ..., A^(n-1)B has full row rank.
short: Inputs must reach every mode of the system.
long: Inputs must reach every mode of the system. The condition is equivalent to the observability of the transposed dual system.
proof: If the rank is deficient, an eigenvector of A^T orthogonal to the reachable subspace cannot be influenced; conversely the Cayley–Hamilton theorem shows the reachable subspace is A-invariant.
consequence: It decides whether pole placement and feedback design are possible.

title: Kalman Observability Rank Condition
subject: Control Theory
statement: A linear system is observable exactly when the stack of C, CA, ..., CA^(n-1) has full column rank.
short: Outputs must reveal every internal mode.
long: Outputs must reveal every internal mode. Unobservable modes cannot be reconstructed from output histories but may still be stable.
proof: If O loses rank, there is a nonzero initial state producing zero output for all time; conversely the Cayley–Hamilton theorem shows the unobservable subspace is A-invariant.
consequence: It is the dual of controllability and governs state-estimator design.

title: Separation Principle for LQG Control
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear system with Gaussian noise and quadratic cost, an optimal output-feedback controller can be built by combining the optimal state-feedback law with an optimal state estimator, and the two designs can be carried out independently.
latex: u=-K\hat x,\qquad \hat x\ \text{from Kalman filter},\qquad J=J_{\text{LQR}}+J_{\text{est}}
short: Estimate first, then control as if the estimate were exact.
long: Estimate first, then control as if the estimate were exact. The separation property relies on linearity, Gaussianity, and the quadratic cost.
proof: Use dynamic programming and the orthogonality of estimation error to the control history to factor the cost.
consequence: It makes stochastic optimal control computationally tractable.

title: Linear Quadratic Regulator and the Riccati Equation
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear system with quadratic cost, the optimal feedback is u = -Kx where K comes from the stabilizing solution of the algebraic Riccati equation.
short: A matrix quadratic equation encodes the value function.
long: A matrix quadratic equation encodes the value function. Stabilizability and detectability guarantee existence of a unique stabilizing positive semidefinite solution.
proof: Substitute a quadratic value function V=x^TPx into the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and minimise over u.
consequence: It is the most widely used optimal control design method.

title: Kalman Filter as Optimal Linear Estimator
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear Gaussian state-space model, the Kalman filter recursively computes the conditional mean and covariance of the state given past observations, minimising mean-square error among all estimators.
short: Predict, compare with measurement, and blend by uncertainty.
long: Predict, compare with measurement, and blend by uncertainty. The gain can be interpreted as a least-squares weight between prediction and observation.
proof: Update the Gaussian conditional distribution using Bayes' rule and propagate its covariance through the linear dynamics.
consequence: It is the standard estimator in navigation, tracking, and time-series analysis.

title: Small-Gain Theorem for Feedback Stability
subject: Control Theory
statement: A feedback interconnection of two stable systems is stable if the product of their induced norms is strictly less than one.
short: The loop must not amplify signals around the cycle.
long: The loop must not amplify signals around the cycle. General versions use gains in different induced norms or nonlinear gain functions.
proof: Write the closed-loop equations, take norms, and apply the contraction mapping principle when the loop gain is below one.
consequence: It is a central robust-stability tool for uncertain systems.

title: Lyapunov Equation for Linear Systems
subject: Control Theory
statement: A Hurwitz matrix A admits, for every positive definite Q, a unique positive definite solution P of the Lyapunov equation, and P certifies stability through the quadratic Lyapunov function x^T P x.
short: Solve a linear matrix equation to get a stability certificate.
long: Solve a linear matrix equation to get a stability certificate. The continuous-time and discrete-time versions use different equations.
proof: Take P as an integral of exp(A^T t) Q exp(A t) over positive time and verify the equation by differentiation.
consequence: It provides computationally tractable stability tests and performance bounds.

title: BIBO Stability and Transfer Function Poles
subject: Control Theory
statement: A rational linear time-invariant system is bounded-input bounded-output stable exactly when all poles of its transfer function lie in the open left half-plane.
short: Stable poles mean bounded responses to bounded inputs.
long: Stable poles mean bounded responses to bounded inputs. Unstable pole-zero cancellations can hide internal instability in the transfer function.
proof: The impulse response is a sum of decaying exponentials when poles are stable, so convolution with a bounded input stays bounded.
consequence: It connects time-domain stability with frequency-domain design.

title: Routh–Hurwitz Stability Criterion
subject: Control Theory
statement: A real polynomial has all roots in the open left half-plane exactly when its Hurwitz determinants are all positive, equivalently when the Routh array has no sign changes in its first column.
short: Coefficients alone decide stability.
long: Coefficients alone decide stability. Necessary conditions include all coefficients having the same sign.
proof: Construct the Hurwitz matrix from the coefficients and use the Cauchy index argument relating root locations to the signs of the determinants.
consequence: It tests stability without computing polynomial roots.

title: Nyquist Stability Criterion
subject: Control Theory
statement: The number of unstable poles of a closed-loop system is determined by the winding number of the open-loop frequency response around the point minus one.
short: Count encirclements to count unstable roots.
long: Count encirclements to count unstable roots. The argument principle links the contour integral of the logarithm to zeros and poles.
proof: Apply the argument principle to 1+G(s) along a contour enclosing the right half-plane.
consequence: It provides gain and phase margin information for robust feedback design.

title: Pontryagin Maximum Principle
subject: Control Theory
statement: For an optimal control problem with state and control constraints, an optimal trajectory admits a costate satisfying adjoint equations and a maximisation condition on the Hamiltonian.
short: Optimality is a two-point boundary problem in state and costate.
long: Optimality is a two-point boundary problem in state and costate. For normal problems the costate multiplier on the running cost is negative, and the Hamiltonian is constant when the dynamics are time-invariant.
proof: Apply a variational argument with needle perturbations of the control and use separation of the resulting cones.
consequence: It is the foundational necessary condition for optimal control.

title: Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman Equation
subject: Control Theory
statement: The value function of a continuous-time optimal control problem satisfies a nonlinear first-order PDE obtained by balancing immediate cost against the change in future value.
short: Dynamic programming becomes a partial differential equation.
long: Dynamic programming becomes a partial differential equation. In deterministic quadratic problems it reduces to the Riccati equation; in stochastic settings a second-order term appears.
proof: Apply the dynamic programming principle over a vanishing time step and expand the value function to first order.
consequence: It connects optimal control, viscosity solutions, and reinforcement learning.

title: Complex Exponentials as LTI Eigenfunctions
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Every complex exponential is an eigenfunction of a linear time-invariant system, with eigenvalue given by the system's frequency response.
latex: x(t)=e^{i\omega t}\ \Rightarrow\ y(t)=H(i\omega)e^{i\omega t},\quad H(i\omega)=\int h(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}d\tau
short: Sinusoids pass through LTI systems unchanged except in amplitude and phase.
long: Sinusoids pass through LTI systems unchanged except in amplitude and phase. The frequency response is the Fourier transform of the impulse response when it exists.
proof: Convolve the exponential with the impulse response and use translation to factor out e^{iomega t}.
consequence: Fourier analysis diagonalises LTI filtering and simplifies system design.

title: Butterworth Filter Magnitude Response
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A Butterworth filter has a magnitude response that is maximally flat in the passband and decreases monotonically to zero in the stopband.
short: No ripple in the passband, at the cost of a gentle roll-off.
long: No ripple in the passband, at the cost of a gentle roll-off. The order n sets the steepness; the cutoff omega_c is the half-power point.
proof: Choose a rational response whose first 2n-1 derivatives vanish at zero, giving a polynomial in omega^2 with a triple structure at the origin.
consequence: It is a standard baseline analog filter prototype.

title: Window Functions and Spectral Leakage
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Truncating a signal to a finite record convolves its spectrum with the Fourier transform of the window, spreading energy into neighbouring frequencies.
short: Finite observation smears sharp spectral lines.
long: Finite observation smears sharp spectral lines. Rectangular windows have high sidelobes; Hann and Hamming windows trade resolution for sidelobe suppression.
proof: Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency by the convolution theorem.
consequence: Window choice controls bias and variance in spectral estimation.

title: Wiener Filter and Mean-Square Optimality
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For stationary signal and noise with known spectra, the linear filter minimising mean-square estimation error has a transfer function given by the signal spectrum divided by the total observed spectrum.
short: Pass frequencies where signal dominates noise.
long: Pass frequencies where signal dominates noise. The causal version requires spectral factorisation of the observation spectrum.
proof: Write the mean-square error as an integral, complete the square pointwise in frequency, and choose H accordingly.
consequence: It is the classical optimum benchmark for denoising and equalisation.

title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter
subject: Signal Processing
statement: The LMS algorithm updates filter coefficients by a small multiple of the instantaneous error times the input vector, approximating stochastic gradient descent on mean-square error.
short: Move the weights slightly against the observed error gradient.
long: Move the weights slightly against the observed error gradient. Convergence and misadjustment depend on the step size and input eigenvalue spread.
proof: The instantaneous gradient of the squared error is -2 e_n x_n; taking a single sample gives an unbiased stochastic gradient step.
consequence: It is simple and widely used in echo cancellation and adaptive equalisation.

title: Matched Filter and Signal-to-Noise Ratio
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For detecting a known waveform in additive white noise, the linear filter maximising output signal-to-noise ratio is matched to a time-reversed copy of the signal.
short: Correlate with the signal you expect.
long: Correlate with the signal you expect. The maximum depends on signal energy but not on its detailed shape.
proof: Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the ratio of the filter output at the sampling time to the noise power.
consequence: It is the optimal receiver for known pulses in radar and communications.

title: Multiresolution Analysis and Wavelet Bases
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A multiresolution analysis is a nested sequence of approximation spaces whose differences yield wavelet subspaces, giving orthonormal bases localised in both scale and position.
latex: V_j\subset V_{j+1},\quad V_{j+1}=V_j\oplus W_j,\quad L^2=\bigoplus_j W_j
short: Approximations at one scale plus details at that scale build the next.
long: Approximations at one scale plus details at that scale build the next. Scaling functions generate V_j and wavelets generate W_j through dilation and translation.
proof: Construct the scaling filter satisfying quadrature-mirror conditions and verify orthonormality of the resulting dilates and translates.
consequence: It gives fast wavelet transforms and sparse representations of piecewise-smooth signals.

title: Total Variation Denoising
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Total variation denoising minimises a fidelity term plus a penalty on the total variation of the signal, suppressing noise while preserving sharp edges.
short: Penalise oscillation, not jumps.
long: Penalise oscillation, not jumps. The solution has piecewise-smooth structure; in one dimension it can be computed exactly by the taut-string algorithm.
proof: Convexity gives a unique solution; optimality is expressed by the divergence of a dual field with modulus at most one.
consequence: It is a foundational method in image restoration and inverse problems.

title: Fisher Information Metric on Statistical Manifolds
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Fisher information matrix defines a Riemannian metric on a parametric family of probability distributions, measuring distinguishability of nearby distributions.
short: Statistical distinguishability is a geometric distance.
long: Statistical distinguishability is a geometric distance. It equals the Hessian of the Kullback–Leibler divergence at coinciding parameters.
proof: Expand the KL divergence to second order in the parameter difference and identify the quadratic form.
consequence: It unifies statistics, information theory, and differential geometry.

title: Amari α-Connections and Dually Flat Manifolds
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A statistical manifold carries a one-parameter family of affine connections; the Levi-Civita connection corresponds to alpha zero, while alpha plus or minus one connections make exponential families dually flat.
short: Different connections capture different statistical structures.
long: Different connections capture different statistical structures. Dual flatness yields generalised Pythagorean theorems for divergences.
proof: Verify that the alpha connections are mutually dual with respect to the Fisher metric and that exponential families have vanishing alpha-one curvature.
consequence: It provides the language of information geometry for inference and optimisation.

title: Natural Gradient Descent
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Preconditioning a gradient by the inverse Fisher information makes optimisation steps invariant to reparametrisation of the statistical model.
short: Move a fixed distance in distribution space, not parameter space.
long: Move a fixed distance in distribution space, not parameter space. It approximates steepest descent with respect to the Fisher–Rao metric.
proof: The Fisher metric transforms covariantly under reparametrisation, so the inverse-metric gradient transforms as a tangent vector.
consequence: It improves conditioning in probabilistic models and reinforcement learning.

title: Information Projection and Pythagorean Identity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: In a dually flat statistical manifold, the KL divergence from an external point to its information projection onto a submanifold decomposes additively, giving a generalised Pythagorean theorem.
short: Projection onto a model splits divergence into two orthogonal parts.
long: Projection onto a model splits divergence into two orthogonal parts. The cross term vanishes because the e-geodesic and m-geodesic meet orthogonally.
proof: Write the KL divergence in exponential-family coordinates and use the orthogonality of the dual geodesics.
consequence: It explains maximum likelihood as information projection and underlies EM geometry.

title: Itô's Lemma for Stochastic Differentials
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: For a smooth function of an Itô diffusion, the differential includes a second-order correction coming from quadratic variation.
short: Stochastic chains get an extra curvature term.
long: Stochastic chains get an extra curvature term. The extra term vanishes for Stratonovich integrals but would make naive chain rule incorrect for Itô integrals.
proof: Taylor expand f, keep terms of order dt from the quadratic variation of Brownian motion, and pass to the limit in probability.
consequence: It is the master formula of stochastic calculus and option pricing.

title: Quadratic Variation of Brownian Motion
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: Along a refining partition the sum of squared increments of Brownian motion converges in probability to the length of the time interval.
short: Brownian paths have infinite variation but finite quadratic variation.
long: Brownian paths have infinite variation but finite quadratic variation. The convergence fails almost surely for arbitrary partitions but holds along refining deterministic partitions.
proof: Compute expectation and variance of the sum using independence of increments and the Gaussian second and fourth moments.
consequence: It creates the second-order term in Itô's formula and underlies realised volatility.

title: Itô Isometry
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The mean square of an Itô integral equals the expectation of the integral of the squared integrand.
short: Itô integrals preserve a scaled L^2 norm.
long: Itô integrals preserve a scaled L^2 norm. The identity extends the definition of the integral from simple processes by completion.
proof: Verify it for simple adapted processes using independence of increments, then pass to limits by density.
consequence: It makes stochastic integration well defined on square-integrable adapted processes.

title: Stratonovich Integral and Chain Rule
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The Stratonovich stochastic integral obeys the ordinary chain rule and arises as the limit of integrals with midpoint evaluation.
short: Midpoint rules preserve the classical calculus identities.
long: Midpoint rules preserve the classical calculus identities. Conversion to Itô form introduces a correction term equal to half the derivative of the diffusion coefficient times its square.
proof: Compare left-endpoint and midpoint Riemann sums; the difference converges to half the quadratic covariation.
consequence: It is preferred in physical models where standard calculus rules should survive.

title: Girsanov Theorem and Measure Change
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: Under suitable integrability, shifting a Brownian motion by a drift can be absorbed by changing to an equivalent probability measure.
short: Drift is a matter of measure.
long: Drift is a matter of measure. Novikov's condition gives a simple sufficient condition for the density to be a true martingale.
proof: Use the stochastic exponential to define the density and verify the martingale property, then check the shifted process has Brownian quadratic variation and independent Gaussian increments.
consequence: It underlies risk-neutral pricing and importance sampling for diffusions.

title: Feynman–Kac Formula
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The solution of a parabolic PDE with a potential term can be represented as the expectation of a functional of a diffusion process.
short: Linear PDEs are averages over random paths.
long: Linear PDEs are averages over random paths. The generator of the diffusion supplies the second-order spatial operator.
proof: Apply Itô's lemma to the product of the PDE solution and the exponential weight, then take expectations and use the martingale property.
consequence: It links PDE theory, stochastic processes, and Monte Carlo computation.

title: Fokker–Planck Equation
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The probability density of a diffusion solves a linear parabolic PDE whose adjoint is the backward Kolmogorov equation.
short: Probability mass flows by drift and diffuses by covariance.
long: Probability mass flows by drift and diffuses by covariance. The stationary density solves the zero-flux equation when detailed balance holds.
proof: Apply Itô's lemma to a test function, take expectations, and integrate by parts to move derivatives onto the density.
consequence: It describes ensemble behaviour in statistical physics, biology, and finance.

title: Tanaka's Formula and Brownian Local Time
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The absolute value of Brownian motion minus its local time at zero is a martingale, generalising Itô's formula to a nonsmooth function.
short: Local time supplies the missing term at a kink.
long: Local time supplies the missing term at a kink. Local time measures the accumulated time the process spends near a given level, normalised by occupation density.
proof: Approximate the absolute value by smooth functions and use the occupation time formula to identify the limit of the second-derivative term.
consequence: It introduces local time and underpins the theory of reflected diffusions.

title: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Process and Stationary Distribution
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process is a mean-reverting diffusion with a Gaussian stationary distribution whose variance balances noise against restoring strength.
short: Noise and mean reversion reach a statistical equilibrium.
long: Noise and mean reversion reach a statistical equilibrium. Its correlation function decays exponentially with rate theta.
proof: Solve the linear SDE explicitly, compute mean and variance, and let time tend to infinity.
consequence: It models thermal fluctuations, interest rates, and velocity in Langevin dynamics.

title: Crystallographic Restriction Theorem
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A rotational symmetry compatible with a two- or three-dimensional periodic lattice can only have order 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6.
short: Lattices forbid fivefold and most other rotations.
long: Lattices forbid fivefold and most other rotations. Quasicrystals evade the restriction by giving up periodicity.
proof: Take a shortest lattice vector and its rotation; their difference is a lattice vector whose length must be at least the minimum, forcing 2 cos theta to be an integer.
consequence: It classifies allowed crystal symmetries and motivated the discovery of quasicrystals.

title: The Seventeen Wallpaper Groups
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: There are exactly seventeen distinct plane crystallographic groups, classified by their translations, rotations, reflections, and glide reflections.
latex: p1,\ p2,\ pm,\ pg,\ cm,\ pmm,\ pmg,\ pgg,\ cmm,\ p4,\ p4m,\ p4g,\ p3,\ p3m1,\ p31m,\ p6,\ p6m
short: Repeating plane patterns fall into seventeen symmetry types.
long: Repeating plane patterns fall into seventeen symmetry types. The classification combines the crystallographic restriction with the possible point groups and lattice shapes.
proof: Bound rotation orders by the crystallographic restriction and enumerate extensions of the translation lattice by the allowed point groups.
consequence: It classifies ornamental patterns and underlies computer vision models of texture.

title: The 230 Three-Dimensional Space Groups
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: There are 230 crystallographic space groups in three dimensions, obtained by combining the 32 point groups with 14 Bravais lattices and nonsymmorphic operations.
short: Three-dimensional crystal symmetry has a finite complete list.
long: Three-dimensional crystal symmetry has a finite complete list. Eleven enantiomorphic pairs among them account for chiral crystal structures.
proof: Classify extensions of the translation group by point groups satisfying compatibility with the lattices, including screw axes and glide planes.
consequence: The list is the language of crystallographic databases and diffraction analysis.

title: Crystal Structure Factor and Electron Density
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The structure factor is the Fourier coefficient of the electron density, so diffraction intensities give its modulus while the phase must be recovered separately.
latex: F(\mathbf k)=\int \rho(\mathbf r)e^{2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}d\mathbf r,\qquad \rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_\mathbf k F(\mathbf k)e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}
short: Diffraction measures Fourier magnitudes of the crystal.
long: Diffraction measures Fourier magnitudes of the crystal. The phase problem is the central obstacle in X-ray crystallography.
proof: Expand the periodic electron density in a Fourier series over the reciprocal lattice and identify coefficients with the scattered amplitudes.
consequence: Fourier inversion reconstructs molecular structures from diffraction data.

title: Bragg's Law of Diffraction
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Constructive reflection from crystal planes occurs when the path difference between waves reflected from successive planes equals an integer number of wavelengths.
short: Planes reflect strongly at angles matching their spacing.
long: Planes reflect strongly at angles matching their spacing. It is equivalent to the Laue condition that the scattering vector belongs to the reciprocal lattice.
proof: The extra path travelled by a ray reflecting from the next plane is 2d sin theta; require it to be an integer multiple of the wavelength.
consequence: It is the basic relation for measuring lattice spacings from diffraction angles.

title: Reciprocal Lattice and the Diffraction Pattern
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The reciprocal lattice consists of wave vectors giving plane waves periodic on the direct lattice, and diffraction peaks occur at those wave vectors.
latex: \mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij},\qquad \mathbf G=h\mathbf b_1+k\mathbf b_2+l\mathbf b_3
short: The diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the lattice.
long: The diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the lattice. The spacing of reciprocal lattice points is inversely proportional to real-space spacing.
proof: A plane wave is periodic under all lattice translations exactly when its wave vector dotted with each lattice vector is a multiple of 2 pi.
consequence: It underlies indexing of diffraction peaks and electronic band structure.

title: Bloch's Theorem for Periodic Potentials
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Eigenfunctions of a Schrödinger operator with a periodic potential are plane waves modulated by a function with the periodicity of the lattice.
latex: \psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad u(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u(\mathbf r)
short: Periodic media have quasi-periodic eigenmodes.
long: Periodic media have quasi-periodic eigenmodes. The crystal momentum k is defined modulo reciprocal lattice vectors.
proof: The translation operators commute with the Hamiltonian, so simultaneous eigenfunctions exist and their translation eigenvalues have modulus one.
consequence: It reduces band-structure calculations to a single unit cell.

title: Brillouin Zones and Band Gaps
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The first Brillouin zone is the Wigner–Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice; energy bands of a periodic Schrödinger operator can have gaps at its boundaries.
latex: BZ=\{\mathbf k:|\mathbf k|\le|\mathbf k-\mathbf G|\ \forall \mathbf G\ne0\}
short: Bragg reflection at zone boundaries opens spectral gaps.
long: Bragg reflection at zone boundaries opens spectral gaps. Degenerate plane waves coupled by a reciprocal lattice vector split in energy.
proof: Restrict the eigenproblem to a two-wave approximation at a zone boundary and diagonalise the resulting two-by-two matrix.
consequence: It explains conductors, semiconductors, and insulators in terms of band structure.

title: Penrose Tilings and Quasicrystalline Order
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Penrose tilings are nonperiodic but ordered planar tilings with sharp diffraction peaks and fivefold symmetry, serving as models for quasicrystals.
short: Order need not imply periodicity.
long: Order need not imply periodicity. Their Fourier spectra contain Bragg peaks at a dense set of wave vectors.
proof: Use the substitution rule based on the golden ratio to build arbitrarily large patches and analyse their Fourier–Bohr spectrum.
consequence: They overturned the assumption that crystals must be periodic.

title: Hückel Molecular Orbital Method
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: In the Hückel approximation, pi-electron molecular orbitals are eigenvectors of a weighted adjacency matrix of the carbon skeleton, with eigenvalues giving orbital energies.
short: Spectral graph theory predicts conjugated-molecule orbitals.
long: Spectral graph theory predicts conjugated-molecule orbitals. Only nearest-neighbour carbon interactions are retained, and overlap integrals are neglected.
proof: Write the linear combination of atomic orbitals equations, set Coulomb integrals to alpha and neighbour resonance integrals to beta, and diagonalise.
consequence: It connects graph spectra to aromatic stability and electron transitions.

title: Pólya Enumeration of Chemical Isomers
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Burnside's lemma and cycle-index generating functions count distinct molecular structures up to the symmetry group of the molecular graph.
short: Average fixed colourings to count unlabelled structures.
long: Average fixed colourings to count unlabelled structures. Pólya's theorem refines the count by tracking the numbers of each substituent.
proof: Count colourings fixed by each group element and average over the group using Burnside's lemma.
consequence: It automates isomer enumeration in computational chemistry.

title: Euler Equations of Inviscid Fluid Flow
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Euler equations express conservation of mass, momentum, and energy for a nonviscous compressible fluid as a system of hyperbolic conservation laws.
short: Newton's laws written for a continuous inviscid medium.
long: Newton's laws written for a continuous inviscid medium. An equation of state closes the system by relating pressure, density, and energy.
proof: Apply integral conservation laws to an arbitrary material volume and use the divergence theorem.
consequence: It is the starting point for compressible aerodynamics and shock-wave theory.

title: Kelvin Circulation Theorem
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: In an inviscid barotropic flow with conservative body forces, the circulation around a material loop is conserved as the loop moves with the fluid.
short: Vortex lines are frozen into an ideal fluid.
long: Vortex lines are frozen into an ideal fluid. Viscosity, non-barotropic thermodynamics, or nonconservative forces break the conservation.
proof: Differentiate the line integral along the material loop, use the Euler equations, and convert the integrand to a perfect differential.
consequence: It underlies vortex dynamics and the persistence of lift in ideal flow.

title: Bernoulli's Theorem for Steady Inviscid Flow
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Along a streamline of a steady inviscid incompressible flow in a conservative force field, the sum of pressure head, kinetic head, and potential head is constant.
short: Pressure drops where speed rises.
long: Pressure drops where speed rises. For irrotational flow the constant is the same on all streamlines.
proof: Project the steady Euler equations along the velocity direction and integrate along the streamline.
consequence: It explains lift, venturi meters, and the pressure distribution around airfoils.

title: Reynolds Number and Dynamic Similarity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The dimensionless Reynolds number comparing inertial to viscous forces determines whether geometrically similar flows behave alike.
short: Same Reynolds number means dynamically similar flow.
long: Same Reynolds number means dynamically similar flow. Low Reynolds number flows are laminar and viscosity-dominated; high Reynolds number flows develop turbulence and thin boundary layers.
proof: Nondimensionalise the Navier–Stokes equations using a length U and velocity scale U, leaving the coefficient 1/Re on the viscous term.
consequence: It justifies wind-tunnel scaling and organises empirical flow regimes.

title: Shallow Water Equations
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The shallow water equations model a thin layer of fluid under gravity by coupling depth-averaged momentum to mass conservation, forming a hyperbolic system with wave speed sqrt(gh).
short: Long gravity waves travel at speed sqrt(g times depth).
long: Long gravity waves travel at speed sqrt(g times depth). They admit shocks interpreted as hydraulic jumps and bore waves.
proof: Integrate the incompressible Euler equations over the thin layer and assume hydrostatic pressure and small vertical acceleration.
consequence: They model tides, tsunamis, and river flooding.

title: Korteweg–de Vries Soliton
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Korteweg–de Vries equation admits solitary travelling waves whose speed is proportional to their amplitude and which survive collisions almost unchanged.
short: Dispersion balances nonlinearity to create a stable pulse.
long: Dispersion balances nonlinearity to create a stable pulse. The equation is integrable and possesses an infinite hierarchy of conserved quantities.
proof: Insert the travelling-wave ansatz, integrate twice using decay at infinity, and verify the sech-squared profile.
consequence: It founded soliton theory with applications to water waves and fibre optics.

title: Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation and Bright Solitons
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation supports bright solitons whose dispersion is exactly balanced by self-focusing nonlinearity.
short: Self-focusing traps the wave against spreading.
long: Self-focusing traps the wave against spreading. The defocusing sign instead supports dark solitons on a nonzero background.
proof: Insert the ansatz into the equation and match real and imaginary parts, using the sech differential equation.
consequence: It models optical fibres, Bose–Einstein condensates, and deep-water envelopes.

title: Burgers' Equation and Shock Formation
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The viscous Burgers equation combines nonlinear steepening with diffusion; in the inviscid limit it develops shock waves selected by the entropy condition.
short: Nonlinearity sharpens waves while viscosity smooths them.
long: Nonlinearity sharpens waves while viscosity smooths them. The Cole–Hopf transform linearises the viscous equation to the heat equation.
proof: Set u = -2 nu (phi_x/phi) to reduce Burgers to the heat equation for phi, then study the zero-viscosity limit.
consequence: It is the simplest model for shock formation and turbulence analogies.

title: Rankine–Hugoniot Conditions
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Across a shock discontinuity, conservation laws require the jump in flux to equal the shock speed times the jump in the conserved quantity.
short: Conservation dictates how fast a discontinuity can move.
long: Conservation dictates how fast a discontinuity can move. An additional entropy condition selects the admissible branch of solutions.
proof: Integrate the conservation law over a shrinking space-time pillbox around the shock and let its width tend to zero.
consequence: It determines shock speeds in gas dynamics and traffic flow.

title: Helmholtz Equation and the Sommerfeld Radiation Condition
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Time-harmonic wave scattering is governed by the Helmholtz equation, and outgoing solutions are selected by requiring decay of the radial derivative in the far field.
short: The radiation condition forbids waves arriving from infinity.
long: The radiation condition forbids waves arriving from infinity. It ensures uniqueness for exterior boundary value problems at real wave numbers.
proof: Expand the solution in outgoing Hankel functions and show the condition excludes the incoming branch.
consequence: It is essential for well-posed acoustic and electromagnetic scattering problems.

title: The Discrete Logarithm Problem in Number Theory
subject: Number Theory
statement: Given a prime p, a generator g of the multiplicative group modulo p and an element h, the discrete logarithm problem asks for an integer x with g^x congruent to h modulo p.
short: Finding exponents modulo a prime is believed to be hard even though exponentiation is easy.
long: Finding exponents modulo a prime is believed to be hard even though exponentiation is easy. The problem is defined in any finite cyclic group, including elliptic curve groups.
proof: Exponentiation is efficiently computable by repeated squaring, while known classical algorithms for inversion, such as baby-step giant-step, require roughly sqrt of the group order operations.
consequence: Its presumed hardness underlies Diffie–Hellman key exchange and ElGamal encryption.

title: Noether's First Theorem on Continuous Symmetries
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system yields a conserved quantity.
short: Symmetry and conservation laws are two sides of one coin.
long: Symmetry and conservation laws are two sides of one coin. Time-translation symmetry gives energy, spatial translation gives momentum, and rotation gives angular momentum.
proof: Invariance of the Lagrangian up to a total derivative implies, via the Euler–Lagrange equations, that a specific combination of momenta and the gauge term is constant along solutions.
consequence: It is the organising principle of modern field theory and explains conservation laws from geometry.

title: The Euler–Lagrange Equations of Variational Calculus
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: A curve that extremises an action integral of the form integral of L(q,q',t) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations on its interior.
short: Extremising an integral gives a differential equation for the extremal curve.
long: Extremising an integral gives a differential equation for the extremal curve. The brachistochrone and minimal surface problems are classical applications.
proof: Consider a variation q+epsilon η vanishing at endpoints, differentiate the action with respect to epsilon at zero, integrate the eta-prime term by parts and use the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations.
consequence: It converts variational principles into the equations of motion of classical mechanics.

title: Hamilton's Canonical Equations of Motion
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In canonical coordinates (q,p), the dynamics of a Hamiltonian system is governed by q-dot equals the partial derivative of H with respect to p and p-dot equals minus the partial derivative with respect to q.
latex: \dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p},\quad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}
short: Hamiltonian mechanics trades second-order equations for a symmetric first-order system.
long: Hamiltonian mechanics trades second-order equations for a symmetric first-order system. Hamilton's equations preserve the symplectic form on phase space.
proof: Apply the Legendre transform to the Lagrangian and vary the phase-space action; integration by parts gives the two canonical equations.
consequence: It is the bridge from classical to quantum mechanics and to symplectic geometry.

title: The Poisson Bracket as a Lie Algebra Structure
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Poisson bracket of functions f and g on phase space is sum over i of (partial f/partial q_i partial g/partial p_i minus partial f/partial p_i partial g/partial q_i), and it satisfies the Jacobi identity.
latex: \{f,g\}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q_i}\right)
short: Observables form a Lie algebra under the Poisson bracket.
long: Observables form a Lie algebra under the Poisson bracket. The time derivative of any observable is its Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian plus an explicit time derivative.
proof: The bracket is bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity by direct differentiation; the evolution formula follows from the chain rule and Hamilton's equations.
consequence: It is the classical counterpart of the quantum commutator.

title: The Legendre Transform and Convex Duality
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Legendre transform of a convex function f is f*(p)=sup over x of (px−f(x)), and for differentiable strictly convex f it is an involution.
short: The Legendre transform swaps a function with the family of its tangent-line intercepts.
long: The Legendre transform swaps a function with the family of its tangent-line intercepts. It converts a Lagrangian into a Hamiltonian and appears throughout convex optimisation.
proof: If f is convex and differentiable, the supremum occurs where p=f'(x); applying the transform again recovers f by the supporting-line characterisation of convexity.
consequence: It is the mathematical engine behind Hamiltonian mechanics and convex duality.

title: The Principle of Stationary Action
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Physical trajectories make the action functional stationary under small variations with fixed endpoints, rather than necessarily minimal.
short: Nature picks paths where first-order changes of the action vanish.
long: Nature picks paths where first-order changes of the action vanish. Stationary includes minima, maxima and saddle points; Fermat's principle of least time is a related variational principle.
proof: For a one-parameter family of paths with fixed endpoints, the first derivative of the action vanishes exactly when the Euler–Lagrange equations hold.
consequence: It unifies mechanics, optics and field theory in a single variational language.

title: The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The state of a nonrelativistic quantum system evolves according to iħ times the time derivative of the wavefunction equals the Hamiltonian operator acting on it.
short: Quantum time evolution is generated by the Hamiltonian through a first-order equation.
long: Quantum time evolution is generated by the Hamiltonian through a first-order equation. For a time-independent Hamiltonian the solution is exp(−iHt/ħ) applied to the initial state.
proof: The equation is a postulate of quantum mechanics; when H is time-independent, exponentiation of the self-adjoint operator gives a unitary evolution group by Stone's theorem.
consequence: It predicts interference, tunnelling and the entire spectroscopy of atoms and molecules.

title: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For position and momentum observables, the product of their standard deviations in any state is at least ħ/2.
short: Position and momentum cannot both be sharply localised.
long: Position and momentum cannot both be sharply localised. The inequality is a consequence of the noncommutation of the corresponding operators and is not a measurement imperfection.
proof:
Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to (X−)ψ and (P−

)ψ and use the commutator [X,P]=iħ.
consequence: It sets fundamental limits on precision and explains the zero-point energy of quantum systems.

title: Canonical Quantisation and the Commutation Relations
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Canonical quantisation replaces classical phase-space variables by operators satisfying [q_i,p_j]=iħ δ_ij and replaces Poisson brackets by commutators divided by iħ.
short: Quantum mechanics is obtained by turning classical brackets into operator commutators.
long: Quantum mechanics is obtained by turning classical brackets into operator commutators. The correspondence is a guiding rule rather than a rigorous functor and has ordering ambiguities for nonlinear expressions.
proof: Dirac's rule identifies the classical Poisson bracket structure with the commutator algebra of observables; the Stone–von Neumann theorem gives uniqueness of the representation for finitely many degrees of freedom.
consequence: It provides the standard route from classical to quantum theories.

title: The Pauli Matrices and Spin-One-half
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The three Pauli matrices are Hermitian 2 by 2 matrices whose pairwise products give i times the remaining matrix; they represent spin-one-half observables and satisfy σ_i σ_j = δ_ij I + i ε_ijk σ_k.
short: A pair of complex matrices encodes the algebra of spin.
long: A pair of complex matrices encodes the algebra of spin. They also generate the fundamental representation of SU(2) and square to the identity.
proof: Direct multiplication of the explicit matrices gives the anticommutation and commutation relations.
consequence: They are the building blocks of two-level quantum systems and of the Dirac equation.

title: The Dirac Equation for Relativistic Spinors
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Dirac equation (i γ^μ ∂_μ − m)ψ=0 is a relativistic wave equation whose gamma matrices satisfy the Clifford algebra relations and whose solutions describe spin-one-half particles and antiparticles.
short: Factoring the relativistic energy relation yields a first-order equation with spin built in.
long: Factoring the relativistic energy relation yields a first-order equation with spin built in. The gamma matrices satisfy {γ^μ,γ^ν}=2η^{μν}I, and squaring the operator recovers the Klein–Gordon equation.
proof: Dirac found matrices whose anticommutators reproduce the Minkowski metric, so applying the conjugate operator gives the relativistic dispersion relation.
consequence: It predicted antimatter and is the foundation of relativistic quantum field theory.

title: Lorentz Transformations and the Invariance of the Speed of Light
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Transformations between inertial frames preserve the spacetime interval c²t²−x²−y²−z² and form the Lorentz group.
short: Different observers disagree about space and time but agree on the spacetime interval.
long: Different observers disagree about space and time but agree on the spacetime interval. They lead to time dilation and length contraction and contain rotations as a subgroup.
proof: Requiring the speed of light to be the same in all inertial frames and the transformations to be linear forces preservation of the Minkowski quadratic form.
consequence: It is the geometric foundation of special relativity.

title: The Stress–Energy Tensor and Local Conservation Laws
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The stress–energy tensor encodes the density and flux of energy and momentum, and its divergence vanishes in the absence of external forces.
short: Local conservation of energy and momentum is expressed by a vanishing divergence.
long: Local conservation of energy and momentum is expressed by a vanishing divergence. In general relativity the partial derivative becomes a covariant derivative, and the tensor acts as the source of gravity.
proof: Noether's theorem applied to spacetime translations yields four conserved currents, assembled into T^{μν}; their divergence vanishes on the equations of motion.
consequence: It is the universal language for energy transport in field theories.

title: Maxwell's Equations in Differential Form
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Using exterior calculus, Maxwell's equations become dF=0 and d star F = J, where F is the electromagnetic field two-form and J the current three-form.
short: The four Maxwell equations compress into two geometric statements.
long: The four Maxwell equations compress into two geometric statements. The first equation implies the existence locally of a potential one-form A with F=dA.
proof: Writing the electric and magnetic fields as components of F and applying the exterior derivative reproduces the homogeneous Maxwell equations; the codifferential gives the inhomogeneous ones.
consequence: This formulation makes gauge invariance and relativistic covariance transparent.

title: Gauge Invariance and Covariant Derivatives
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Replacing ordinary derivatives by covariant derivatives built from a connection makes field equations invariant under local symmetry transformations.
short: Gauge fields compensate for spacetime-dependent symmetry rotations.
long: Gauge fields compensate for spacetime-dependent symmetry rotations. The curvature of the connection is the gauge field strength.
proof: Under a local gauge transformation the connection changes inhomogeneously so that D_μψ transforms covariantly; the commutator of covariant derivatives gives the curvature, which transforms homogeneously.
consequence: It is the common structure underlying electromagnetism, Yang–Mills theory and general relativity.

title: The Aharonov–Bohm Effect
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Charged particles can be affected by an electromagnetic potential in a region where the electric and magnetic fields vanish, through the topology of the configuration space.
short: Even with zero field, a nontrivial potential can shift quantum phases.
long: Even with zero field, a nontrivial potential can shift quantum phases. It demonstrates that gauge potentials have physical significance beyond the classical fields.
proof: Electrons travelling around a solenoid enclosing magnetic flux acquire a relative phase equal to the enclosed flux in appropriate units, producing a measurable interference shift.
consequence: It reveals the role of topology and holonomy in quantum physics.

title: Yang–Mills Gauge Theory and Field Strength
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Yang–Mills theory generalises electromagnetism to nonabelian gauge groups, with field strength given by the curvature F=dA+A∧A and equations D star F=0.
short: Noncommuting gauge symmetries produce self-interacting force fields.
long: Noncommuting gauge symmetries produce self-interacting force fields. The nonabelian term A∧A is what makes the theory nonlinear.
proof: The field strength arises as the commutator of covariant derivatives, and the Yang–Mills equations are the Euler–Lagrange equations of the action integral of tr(F∧star F).
consequence: It describes the strong and weak nuclear interactions.

title: The Gauge Group of the Standard Model
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Standard Model of particle physics is based on the gauge group SU(3) times SU(2) times U(1), describing the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions.
short: Three symmetry groups organise all known elementary particles and forces except gravity.
long: Three symmetry groups organise all known elementary particles and forces except gravity. Spontaneous symmetry breaking reduces the electroweak part to electromagnetic U(1).
proof: Matter fields are assigned representations of the group; requiring local gauge invariance forces the introduction of gauge bosons transforming under the adjoint representation.
consequence: It is the most thoroughly tested framework in fundamental physics.

title: The Boltzmann Transport Equation
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Boltzmann equation describes the evolution of the distribution of particles in phase space under streaming and collisions.
short: It is the kinetic-theory analogue of a conservation law with a collision term.
long: It is the kinetic-theory analogue of a conservation law with a collision term. The collision operator drives the distribution toward local thermodynamic equilibrium.
proof: Balance of particles in a phase-space volume gives the streaming terms; modelling collisions by a bilinear integral operator gives C[f].
consequence: It underlies transport coefficients, hydrodynamic limits and the H-theorem.

title: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In an isolated system, thermodynamic entropy never decreases; in statistical mechanics entropy is proportional to the logarithm of the number of accessible microstates.
short: Disorder grows because there are overwhelmingly more disordered configurations.
long: Disorder grows because there are overwhelmingly more disordered configurations. Boltzmann's H-theorem gives a mechanical account of entropy increase under molecular chaos assumptions.
proof: The logarithm makes entropy additive for independent systems; the overwhelming dominance of high-multiplicity macrostates explains the observed increase.
consequence: It sets the arrow of time and limits the efficiency of heat engines.

title: The Partition Function of Statistical Mechanics
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The partition function is the weighted sum over states of exp(−beta times energy), and thermodynamic quantities are obtained from its derivatives with respect to beta.
short: One generating function encodes the entire equilibrium thermodynamics.
long: One generating function encodes the entire equilibrium thermodynamics. The canonical ensemble assigns probabilities proportional to exp(−βE_s).
proof: Maximising entropy subject to fixed average energy gives the Boltzmann distribution, whose normalisation is Z; differentiating log Z gives averages and fluctuations.
consequence: It connects microscopic Hamiltonians to measurable thermodynamic quantities.

title: The Ising Model of Ferromagnetism
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Ising model assigns spins ±1 to lattice sites with energy minus the sum of couplings times neighbouring products, and it exhibits a phase transition in two or more dimensions.
short: A lattice of tiny magnets is the simplest model of spontaneous order.
long: A lattice of tiny magnets is the simplest model of spontaneous order. The one-dimensional model has no finite-temperature phase transition, while the two-dimensional model was solved exactly by Onsager.
proof: The transfer-matrix method reduces the partition function to the largest eigenvalue of a finite matrix; in one dimension no singularity appears for positive temperature, while in two dimensions a critical temperature emerges.
consequence: It is the paradigmatic model for critical phenomena and phase transitions.

title: Phase Transitions and Critical Exponents
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Near a continuous phase transition, thermodynamic quantities follow power laws whose exponents are universal across broad classes of materials.
short: Different materials share the same numerical exponents near criticality.
long: Different materials share the same numerical exponents near criticality. Universality classes depend only on dimensionality, symmetry and range of interactions.
proof: The renormalisation group explains critical exponents as eigenvalues of a linearised flow near a fixed point, which depends only on coarse features of the system.
consequence: It explains why seemingly unrelated systems behave identically at criticality.

title: The Renormalisation Group and Scaling
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The renormalisation group studies how a physical theory changes as the energy or length scale is varied, integrating out short-distance degrees of freedom.
short: Physics at one scale determines the effective laws at another.
long: Physics at one scale determines the effective laws at another. Fixed points of the flow govern critical phenomena and continuum limits.
proof: Rescale coordinates and fields, integrate over a momentum shell and absorb the change into running couplings; iterating gives a flow equation for the couplings.
consequence: It underlies critical phenomena, quantum field theory and the predictive power of effective field theories.

title: Feynman's Path Integral Formulation
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The quantum amplitude to go from one configuration to another is a sum over all paths weighted by exp(i times the action divided by ħ).
short: Quantum mechanics sums over every possible path, not just the classical one.
long: Quantum mechanics sums over every possible path, not just the classical one. In the classical limit, stationary-phase contributions from paths near the classical trajectory dominate.
proof: Discretising time gives a product of short-time kernels and an ordinary multidimensional integral; the continuum limit is the formal path integral, which can be made rigorous in Euclidean signature for many theories.
consequence: It is the standard language of quantum field theory and tunnelling calculations.

title: The WKB Approximation for Slowly Varying Potentials
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For a one-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a potential varying slowly compared with the wavelength, the wavefunction is approximately a rapidly oscillating exponential whose local wavenumber is set by the classical momentum.
short: Quantum waves locally behave like rays of classical particles.
long: Quantum waves locally behave like rays of classical particles. Connection formulas at turning points relate the decaying and oscillatory regions and give tunnelling rates.
proof: Insert an ansatz of the form amplitude times exponential of phase divided by ħ into the Schrödinger equation and equate powers of ħ; the leading order gives the Hamilton–Jacobi equation.
consequence: It explains tunnelling, semiclassical spectra and the correspondence principle.

title: Perturbation Theory and Feynman Diagrams
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Weakly interacting quantum field theories can be expanded in a power series in the coupling constant whose terms are represented graphically by Feynman diagrams.
short: Complex interaction integrals become a bookkeeping game with diagrams.
long: Complex interaction integrals become a bookkeeping game with diagrams. Each diagram encodes a momentum-space integral and carries a symmetry factor.
proof: Expand the interacting exponential in the path integral and apply Wick's theorem to express correlation functions as sums over contractions, indexed by diagrams.
consequence: It produces the spectacularly accurate predictions of quantum electrodynamics.

title: The Einstein Field Equations of General Relativity
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The curvature of spacetime is related to its matter content by the equation relating the Einstein tensor to the stress–energy tensor.
short: Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and curvature tells matter how to move.
long: Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and curvature tells matter how to move. The equations reduce to Newtonian gravity in the weak-field, slow-motion limit.
proof: They follow from varying the Einstein–Hilbert action plus a matter action; the left side is the unique divergence-free symmetric tensor built from the metric and its first two derivatives.
consequence: It predicts gravitational lensing, black holes and gravitational waves.

title: The Schwarzschild Solution and Black Holes
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations describes the exterior field of a nonrotating mass and contains an event horizon at the Schwarzschild radius.
short: A static spherical mass bends spacetime so strongly that a horizon can form.
long: A static spherical mass bends spacetime so strongly that a horizon can form. Birkhoff's theorem guarantees uniqueness among spherically symmetric vacuum solutions.
proof: Impose spherical symmetry and staticity on the metric, insert into the vacuum field equations and solve the resulting ordinary differential equations with the Newtonian limit fixing the integration constant.
consequence: It predicted black holes and the correct perihelion precession of Mercury.

title: The Virial Theorem for Bound Systems
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For a stable bound system with potential energy homogeneous of degree k, twice the time-averaged kinetic energy equals k times the time-averaged potential energy.
short: Bound systems balance motion and interaction in a fixed ratio.
long: Bound systems balance motion and interaction in a fixed ratio. For gravity and electrostatics k=−1, giving 2<T>=−<V>.
proof: The second derivative of the moment of inertia is bounded for a bound system; using the equations of motion makes its average equal to 4<T>+2<V>, which must vanish.
consequence: It estimates masses of galaxy clusters and relates kinetic and potential energies in molecular systems.

title: Weyl's Law for Eigenvalues of the Laplacian
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For a bounded domain, the number of Dirichlet eigenvalues of the Laplacian below λ grows asymptotically like the volume of the domain times λ^{d/2} divided by the appropriate power of 4π.
short: High-frequency spectral density counts the volume in phase space.
long: High-frequency spectral density counts the volume in phase space. The second term in the expansion contains the boundary area and leads to the Weyl conjecture.
proof: Approximate the eigenvalue counting function by the trace of the heat kernel, use the short-time heat kernel asymptotics with leading coefficient the volume, and apply a Tauberian theorem.
consequence: It connects geometry and spectrum and is the starting point of spectral geometry.

title: The Picard–Lindelöf Existence and Uniqueness Theorem
subject: Differential Equations
statement: If the right-hand side of an initial value problem is continuous and Lipschitz in the state variable near the initial point, there is a unique solution on some interval around that point.
short: Lipschitz continuity prevents solution curves from branching.
long: Lipschitz continuity prevents solution curves from branching. Continuity alone gives existence by Peano's theorem but not uniqueness.
proof: Rewrite the problem as an integral equation and show the Picard iteration operator is a contraction on a small closed interval in a suitable weighted sup norm; Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique fixed point.
consequence: It is the fundamental well-posedness result for ordinary differential equations.

title: Picard Iteration for Initial Value Problems
subject: Differential Equations
statement: Starting from the constant initial guess, repeatedly integrate the right-hand side along the previous approximate solution to generate a sequence converging to the unique solution.
short: Turn the differential equation into an integral equation and iterate.
long: Turn the differential equation into an integral equation and iterate. For linear equations the iterates converge on the whole interval of existence.
proof: The iteration is a contraction in a suitable norm by the Picard–Lindelöf estimates, so Banach's theorem gives convergence to the unique fixed point, which solves the integral equation.
consequence: It provides both a constructive existence proof and a practical symbolic solution method.

title: Grönwall's Inequality for Differential Inequalities
subject: Differential Equations
statement: If a nonnegative function satisfies an integral inequality bounded by a constant plus the integral of a coefficient times the function, then it is bounded by the constant times an exponential of the accumulated coefficient.
latex: u(t)\le C+\int_0^t a(s)u(s)ds \Rightarrow u(t)\le C e^{\int_0^t a(s)ds}
short: Growth rates bounded in integral form produce exponential bounds.
long: Growth rates bounded in integral form produce exponential bounds. The differential form u' ≤ a u with u(0)=C gives the same conclusion.
proof: Let v(t) be the right-hand integral bound; then v'=a u ≤ a v and v(0)=C, so multiplying by exp(−integral a) shows v is nonincreasing after normalisation.
consequence: It proves continuous dependence on initial data and uniqueness in ODE theory.

title: The Wronskian Test for Linear Independence of Solutions
subject: Differential Equations
statement: Solutions of a linear homogeneous ODE are linearly independent if their Wronskian determinant is nonzero at some point of the interval.
short: A determinant of solutions and their derivatives detects independence.
long: A determinant of solutions and their derivatives detects independence. For solutions of a linear equation the Wronskian is either identically zero or never zero, by Abel's identity.
proof: If the Wronskian is nonzero at a point, the linear system for coefficients in a vanishing linear combination has only the trivial solution, so the functions are independent.
consequence: It lets one decide when a set of known solutions forms a fundamental system.

title: Variation of Parameters for Linear ODEs
subject: Differential Equations
statement: A particular solution of a linear nonhomogeneous ODE can be built by replacing the constants in the general homogeneous solution with functions determined by a linear system.
short: Let the coefficients of the homogeneous basis vary to absorb the forcing term.
long: Let the coefficients of the homogeneous basis vary to absorb the forcing term. Imposing a normalisation condition gives a unique system for the derivatives u_i'.
proof: Substituting y_p into the equation, the extra condition on the u_i' eliminates their second derivatives, leaving a linear algebraic system solved by Cramer's rule using the Wronskian.
consequence: It produces particular solutions for arbitrary forcing terms once the homogeneous solution is known.

title: Reduction of Order for a Known Solution
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For a second-order linear homogeneous ODE, knowing one nonzero solution y_1 allows reduction to a first-order equation by substituting y=v y_1.
short: One known solution lowers a second-order problem to first order.
long: One known solution lowers a second-order problem to first order. The formula follows from Abel's identity for the Wronskian.
proof: Substituting y=v y_1 and using that y_1 solves the equation leaves an equation in v' only, which is first-order linear and solvable by an integrating factor.
consequence: It completes the fundamental solution set when only one solution is known.

title: The Method of Undetermined Coefficients
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For linear constant-coefficient ODEs with polynomial, exponential or sinusoidal forcing, guess a particular solution of the same functional form with unknown coefficients and solve for them.
latex: L[y]=g \Rightarrow y_p \text{ of the form of } g
short: Guess the shape of the answer, then determine the constants.
long: Guess the shape of the answer, then determine the constants. If the guess duplicates a homogeneous solution, multiply by a suitable power of x.
proof: Differentiation preserves the family of polynomials times exponentials times sinusoids, so applying L maps a finite-dimensional ansatz space into itself and gives a linear system for the coefficients.
consequence: It is the fastest hand method for many forced oscillatory and growth-decay problems.

title: Phase Line Analysis of One-Dimensional Autonomous Equations
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For x'=f(x), equilibria are the zeros of f and their stability is determined by the sign of f on either side.
short: A sign diagram of f tells the whole qualitative story in one dimension.
long: A sign diagram of f tells the whole qualitative story in one dimension. An equilibrium is stable if f points toward it from both sides and unstable if f points away.
proof: Solutions are monotone between equilibria because f has constant sign there, so the direction arrows determine global behaviour.
consequence: It is the simplest example of the qualitative theory of dynamical systems.

title: The Logistic Differential Equation and Carrying Capacity
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The logistic equation x'=rx(1−x/K) has equilibrium solutions 0 and K, with K asymptotically stable for positive r, and its solutions are explicit sigmoid curves.
short: Growth slows as a population approaches its carrying capacity.
long: Growth slows as a population approaches its carrying capacity. The solution starting below K increases monotonically to K and never exceeds it.
proof: Separating variables and using partial fractions gives x(t)=K/(1+Ce^{-rt}), whose limit as t grows is K.
consequence: It is the standard model for saturating population growth and diffusion of innovations.

title: The Lotka–Volterra Predator–Prey Equations
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The system x'=ax−bxy, y'=dxy−cy has a nonconstant first integral, so its positive solutions are closed orbits around the coexistence equilibrium.
short: Predator and prey populations oscillate around a stable centre.
long: Predator and prey populations oscillate around a stable centre. The orbits are level sets of dx log x − b x + c y log y − d y, and their period depends on the amplitude.
proof: Eliminate time by dividing the equations; the resulting separable equation gives a conserved quantity whose level curves in the positive quadrant are closed.
consequence: It is the foundational model of mathematical ecology.

title: The SIR Compartmental Epidemic Model
subject: Differential Equations
statement: The SIR model splits a population into susceptible, infected and recovered classes with equations S'=−βSI/N, I'=βSI/N−γI, R'=γI, and an epidemic occurs when β/γ exceeds one.
short: An outbreak grows only if each infected person infects more than one other on average.
long: An outbreak grows only if each infected person infects more than one other on average. The basic reproduction number R_0=β/γ determines the initial growth and the final epidemic size.
proof: Linearising the infected equation near the disease-free equilibrium gives growth rate β−γ, so the threshold is R_0=1; a first integral relates S and I and gives the final size relation.
consequence: It underlies vaccination thresholds and public-health forecasting.

title: The Poincaré–Bendixson Theorem in the Plane
subject: Differential Equations
statement: A nonempty compact limit set of a planar flow containing no equilibrium is a periodic orbit.
short: In two dimensions, long-term motion that avoids equilibria must be periodic.
long: In two dimensions, long-term motion that avoids equilibria must be periodic. The result fails in three or more dimensions, where strange attractors can occur.
proof: A transversal through the limit set is crossed repeatedly; the return map is monotone and order-preserving, so its recurrence forces a fixed point corresponding to a closed orbit.
consequence: It rules out chaos in continuous planar systems and characterises limit cycles.

title: The Hartman–Grobman Linearisation Theorem
subject: Differential Equations
statement: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium, a smooth flow is topologically conjugate to its linearisation.
short: For hyperbolic equilibria, the linear approximation gets the local picture right.
long: For hyperbolic equilibria, the linear approximation gets the local picture right. Hyperbolicity means no eigenvalue of the linearisation has zero real part; nonhyperbolic points require higher-order analysis.
proof: Construct a conjugacy by matching orbit segments through a small box around the equilibrium, using the contraction mapping principle on the resulting functional equation.
consequence: It justifies linear stability analysis for equilibria.

title: Lyapunov's Direct Method for Stability
subject: Differential Equations
statement: If there is a positive definite function whose derivative along trajectories is negative definite near an equilibrium, that equilibrium is asymptotically stable.
short: A decreasing energy-like function proves stability without solving the equation.
long: A decreasing energy-like function proves stability without solving the equation. Lyapunov functions are the nonlinear analogue of energy in mechanical systems.
proof: Sublevel sets of V are small neighbourhoods of the equilibrium; since V decreases strictly, trajectories cannot leave them and must approach the equilibrium by LaSalle's invariance principle.
consequence: It is the main tool for stability analysis in nonlinear control and dynamical systems.

title: The Saddle-Node Bifurcation of Equilibria
subject: Differential Equations
statement: In a saddle-node bifurcation, two equilibria collide and annihilate as a parameter crosses a critical value, with normal form x'=μ+x².
short: A pair of fixed points is born or dies as a parameter is tuned.
